#1024. What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump

From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. So can the Democrats now make a difference?

For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one issue ranked above all others: the economy.

So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?

Markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory.

With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a note.

"I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind."

Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.

Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, said the vote showed the extent of that opposition.  Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.

"This election shows that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he said. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted."

If the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown said, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.

According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center, 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.

That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.

Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.

"Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office."

Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.

Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.

Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard said, the scale of the Republicans' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.

Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.

Were a deal to be struck with Iran, soaring energy prices — a pivotal election issue — could finally fall, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.

"You've got to get a deal with Iran, and you've got to bring down gas prices," Kirkegaard said. "From a political point of view, that's the most important thing now."

George Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he said in a note.

Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.

Yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another issue vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.

That raises the prospect of the new Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic issues to secure his political survival.

"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," Kirkegaard said. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs."

Despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle in trying to reverse them.

#1023. European shares join a global sell-off as AI spending fears rattle Wall Street and Asian markets

European shares have fallen after sharp losses in Asia and on Wall Street. Doubts over huge AI investments and fears of curbs following the Democrats' US midterm victory have rattled global markets.

European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.

European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks.

Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.

Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.

Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

#1022. From young players to women's game to the national team, how can SFA duo Maxwell and Mulholland possibly be trusted to move things forward?

Published: 13:33 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 15:30 EST, 27 November 2026

With the Scottish FA’s widely trumpeted plan to get young players more game time now lying in a ditch off the M74, it was hard not to raise a wry smile at the midweek communique from Hampden over the intention to come up with some other kind of just-as-good idea somewhere in the new year.

‘Given the implications for our game, and our young talent, it is imperative that we take the necessary time to get those proposals right,’ it closed.

Bit late for that chat, is it not? Shouldn’t that work behind the scenes have been done before the grand summit at St Andrews back at the start of September when SFA chief executive Ian Maxwell and his chief football officer Craig Mulholland announced themselves lords and saviours of the national game with their scheme to shoehorn Under-21 players – no matter how good, bad or indifferent they may be – into club sides all over the country?

It all sounded good at the time, of course, if you put your head in the clouds and daydreamed over how pretty the world might be if everyone just got along.

Handwringers nationwide fell over themselves to simper the usual platitudes over how self-interest must be sacrificed for the greater good. There was probably some kind of online petition to link hands between all 42 senior grounds for a chorus of Kumbaya.

Meanwhile, anyone who has the faintest idea of the realpolitik of Scottish football looked at what was on the table and knew it was destined for the knacker’s yard.

SFA top brass Craig Mulholland and Ian Maxwell flank Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli

The SFA should have been consulting their more prominent clubs before going public over what might work and what might not, moulding something that the teams which matter were willing to support.

Instead, almost half the outfits in the Premiership blew their proposals out of the water in the end.

The sound of silence from Hampden, of course, had already become deafening as they realised they’d made a pig’s ear of it. Right now, it looks like everyone is back to the drawing board.

It’s embarrassing for the SFA. It has just made Maxwell and Mulholland look like they are incapable of taking the game with them on important matters.

Naturally, though, there wasn’t a single word from Haudit or Daudit in that press release to more or less confirm a major reverse ferret is going to be required. When things go belly-up, the high heid yins at Hampden are often nowhere to be seen.

Maxwell was too busy turning his mind to other matters during the week anyway, namely the fact that Scotland will be co-hosting the Women’s World Cup with the rest of the UK in 2035.

Given that was the only actual bid, the award of the event was hardly earth-shattering, but that didn’t stop Maxwell treating it as his Next Big Thing.

Maxwell has been in position at the SFA for more than eight years but has lacked real impact

‘I think it is going to be an absolutely transformational event to host in the UK and Ireland,’ he gushed. ‘The hard work starts now in terms of legacy and impact and driving everything we can from it.’

Hmmmm. Nice as it is that he’s managed to put being custard-pied at home by a large chunk of the Premiership over youth opportunities behind him, it might be wise to take Maxwell’s words over the women’s game with a pinch of salt.

He also called Scotland going to their first World Cup in 2019 ‘transformational’. Months later, Glasgow City won their 13th straight title with a ten-goal win over Motherwell on a council-run pitch in Wishaw in front of 100 people with no shelter, no seating and no obvious way for an ambulance to gain entry should a medical emergency occur. One Motherwell player had to nick across to the attached sports centre to get a chair for an injured team-mate to sit on.

A year had passed since the national team’s qualification, but there was still no kind of plan for the £400,000 prize money that they earned.

City’s Hayley Lauder, who’d been at the World Cup in France, tweeted: ‘Just won a league title in a public park at a sports centre. Not how I envisaged the game in 2019.’

It was a message that encapsulated the catastrophic failure to build on the incredible platform France 2019 provided under Maxwell’s reign.

Scotland celebrate an Erin Cuthbert goal against Argentina in 2019 before it all turned sour

That should have been the real launchpad for the women’s game here. Instead, it turned into a toxic shambles that killed any kind of momentum.

Progress since has been nothing like what it should have been. The national team, out to reach the next World Cup in next week’s play-off against Sweden, has been mired in failure. The women’s game lives back in the shadows amid pitiful attendances and an inability – or, it sometimes seems, refusal – to sell itself.

Yet, it could all have been so different. Just remember the scene back in ‘19. Scotland have to beat Argentina to make the last 16. A TV audience of six million watched the meeting with England earlier in the campaign.

The drama as Shelley Kerr’s side let slip a three-goal lead with 16 minutes to play – eventually drawing 3-3 thanks to a stoppage-time penalty retaken after an initial save by keeper Lee Gibson – was just incredible. It was the talk of the nation the next day.

And, then, it all just died a death. The head coach Shelley Kerr eventually coughed to the fact ‘a few drinks’ had been taken before a debrief the next day that reportedly left some players in tears.

No one wanted to talk about it. No one ever has, really. Yours truly asked Glasgow City for an interview with Gibson, then Alexander, in the early stages of the following season.

Top-flight matches between teams in the SWPL regularly take place on glorified public pitches

She’d been at the centre of a major global event. There was a story to be told. City insisted all requests had to be run past the SFA and their media office pretty much made it clear it wouldn’t be happening before she had even been asked.

No one told their stories of the biggest event in the history of women’s football here. Not properly. It felt like some kind of Omerta had been put in place over it.

Kerr, inexplicably, was allowed to keep her job by Maxwell and then failed to make it to Euro 2022. Instead, that year was marked by the women’s team, with Kerr gone, threatening to take legal action against the SFA over a lack of resources – with then captain Rachel Corsie referring to ‘years of iniquity, disrespect, and, in some cases, abuse.’

Yeah, the aftermath of France 2019 was ‘transformational’ all right. It transformed the hundreds of thousands of folk compelled to watch women’s football on national TV that summer back into people who forget it even exists.

Colleagues tell me there was no scope midweek to even interview anyone in a position of power within the SFA over what should have been a Good News Story regarding 2035. Hardly ‘driving everything we can from it’, is it?

I mean, how can you trust the likes of Maxwell to harness the opportunities afforded by that event – or Euro 2028 on home soil – when reflecting upon the raging binfire France 2019 became?

Mulholland is a regular sight being entertained by football matches up and down the country

How can you trust him and Mulholland to get it right on forging pathways for young players when they made such a Horlicks of trying to implement that poorly-planned proposal for Scotland-eligible Under-21s and failed again when changing it to involve Under-23s?

There’s a far wider issue with the production of players that involves going deep into the SFA’s own workings, addressing that lack of knowledge St Mirren boss Craig McLeish talked about at the lower levels of grassroots.

Indeed, there are problems all over the SFA. With refereeing standards. With VAR. With Steve Clarke admitting he forced the top brass into ‘panicking’ before the World Cup and giving him a new four-year deal.

If Maxwell and Mulholland’s blue-eyed boy Sebastien Pocognoli doesn’t start looking like he’s got a handle on his role as Clarke’s successor as national boss after a grim start to his reign, everything points to the two of them having to go the same way as their original Youth Plan. By being binned.

#1021. Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

Evidence suggests exercise can keep more cancer patients alive. But what does "living longer" actually mean, and who does it apply to?

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.   In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.

Oliver Glasner has played down the significance of his warning to Nottingham Forest’s squad after their defeat at Brentford has had the desired impact.

The Austrian said last weekend there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

Speaking this week, he said: “I didn’t attack anyone directly. We share that we want to be successful and win games. It was not a problem.

“It was much louder outside than I felt it was inside. This is just how I see a relationship has to be. Let’s talk about things if we don’t like things.

“If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

The City manager added: “It is quite easy with him because he recognises any mistake immediately. I’ve spoken to him about it, but I didn’t feel the need to be so deep with him because he already knows and recognises that he has made some mistakes.”

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca said: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

“We know exactly what we are doing well and what we need to improve. It is just a matter of time.”

#1017. Dengue has exploded globally with shocking speed

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

A pregnant person with dengue speaks to a nurse in Peru, which has been hit by a surge of cases this year. Credit: Juan Carlos Cisneros/AFP/Getty

The debilitating viral disease called dengue has exploded in incidence far more than previously thought, a new analysis suggests.

The number of reported global cases of dengue, which is transmitted by infected mosquitoes, rose from 430,000 in 1990 to 14.7 million in 2024 — a 34-fold increase, the analysis says.

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

The data were presented on 22 November at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH) in National Harbor, Maryland. Scientists also provided some of the strongest results yet about a counter-intuitive way to curb the disease’s staggering spread: the release of specially modified mosquitoes. But researchers also presented discouraging data on other solutions, and scientists at the meeting emphasized that the campaign to beat back dengue will be complicated and costly.

“We’re in an extraordinary and pivotal moment” in the history of studying mosquito-borne illnesses, said Albert Ko, president of ASTMH. Trial results presented at the meeting showed, he said, that “we can get rigorous evidence on what works, what doesn’t and what needs to be done to scale these effective interventions to protect the 4 billion people” around the world who are exposed to dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses.

Dengue causes fever, headaches and severe bone pain. It is transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti, a species of mosquito that thrives in warm, urban environments. Global warming and increased urbanization have expanded the mosquitoes’ range. Existing vaccines provide imperfect protection.

Cases of dengue are often recorded in disparate databases that aren’t easily comparable, says Ahyoung Lim, an infectious-disease modeler at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who was involved in the study on dengue incidence. The results have also been published as a preprint1 on Research Square ahead of peer review. This has meant that no single database has captured the total number of reported dengue cases over time, leading Lim and her team to compile the most complete record of reported cases and use statistical modelling tools to fill in gaps in which data were missing.

The staggering increase in reported cases isn’t surprising, says Eng Eong Ooi, a dengue virologist at Duke–NUS Medical School in Singapore, who was not involved in the research. Populations in urban environments around the world are steadily increasing, he says, which means that “more and more people are living at risk of dengue each year”.

One promising approach to curb dengue starts with breeding mosquitoes and deliberately infecting them with a bacterium called Wolbachia that reduces the insects’ ability to transmit viruses. When released into the wild, these infected mosquitoes pass the bacterium on to their offspring, eventually lowering the number of highly transmissive mosquitoes.

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

At the ASTMH meeting, another team of researchers shared results from the first randomized controlled trial in the Americas to test Wolbachia’s effect on dengue transmission. Between January 2021 and May 2022, the researchers released roughly 32 million Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes across designated regions of Brazil and monitored almost 6,000 children living inside and outside these regions. The children provided annual blood samples between 2020 and 2024, and the reseachers found that those in the Wolbachia regions were 68% less likely to be infected with dengue compared with those in non-Wolbachia regions.

These positive results mark an important milestone in proving Wolbachia’s potential to drastically reduce dengue cases, says Elisabeth Nelson, an epidemiologist at the Yale School of Public Health in New Haven, Connecticut, and a researcher on the trial.

#1015. Farm that became a football factory: Club where Man United, Liverpool, Man City, Leeds and Ireland legends started out is back in national Cup final... and hoping it's the first of many more glory days

Published: 16:16 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 16:26 EST, 27 November 2026

Gavin Whelan had been away from the domestic game for a while and hadn’t really been looking for a way back in.

The former Drogheda United and Bray Wanderers player had stepped away from the League of Ireland at 29 and his involvement in football in the past few years had been restricted to helping coach his older son Jayden’s team as they went through the age grades at Home Farm – the fourth generation of the Whelan family to come through the club.

The Whelan dynasty, with Gavin second from right beside his uncle Ronnie (centre) and Paul (seond from left)

But when it emerged the FAI were setting up a third tier, he had a chat with Brian Honohan, who had been a Shamrock Rovers teammate of his father, Paul, and they decided to put together a group that would help put Home Farm back where they belong.

This inaugural National League final in Carlisle Grounds is a step in that direction. Home Farm face Lucan United, who beat them 2-0 in Whitehall recently in the group stages. In a way, it is like the old meeting the new although the fact that two Dublin clubs are contesting the first final in a concept that was supposed to broaden the league’s base to uncharted territories will be viewed a little sceptically.

But that shouldn’t take away from what both Home Farm and Lucan are trying to do – or the sense of camaraderie and purpose that has characterised the first truncated season of the third tier.

Clubs have become comrades in what they are trying to do – right down to ensuring each visiting team would sit down for a meal after the final whistle before beginning the journey home.

‘There has been a sense that we all have to help each other, that we are all in this together,’ says Home Farm chairman Brendan Menton.

‘So, the clubs would organise something to eat for the visiting team. It meant that if Bonagee had to go back up the road to Donegal, they wouldn’t need to stop off somewhere. It was a small thing, but it has built a real sense of togetherness among all 15 clubs.’

Nicola Brannigan (second from left), Brendan Menton (centre), Richard Dunne (second right) and Gavin Peers (right)

Brendan Menton senior was one of the founders of Home Farm back in 1928

Menton is a former chief executive of the FAI, holding that position during Saipan in 2002. But his footballing roots have been in Home Farm.

Like Whelan, Menton’s family have four generations who have lined out for the famous nursery – with his two grandchildren currently part of the underage teams. And his father, Brendan senior, was one of the founding members of the club back in 1928.

The club came into existence when Leo Fitzmaurice, concerned about the lack of recreational facilities for young people in the Drumcondra and Whitehall area, decided to set up a street league.

Home Farm Road, which is a street in the locality, was one of the roads that formed a team.

‘My father was one of the founding members of the club, who were established to play in the Drumcondra and Whitehall street league. My family lived on 31 Home Farm Road, the name came from a Monastery that was on Iona Road and back a few centuries ago, every Monastery had their own home farm and that’s where the name came from.

‘The story goes that one Friday evening, some boys from the Richmond Road team, which included Don Seery, came to play Home Farm Road but their ball burst so the two teams decided to amalgamate and from that, the club was born.’

And from such uncertain beginnings grew one of the most successful schoolboy clubs in Ireland. More than 50 Irish internationals have passed through its famous nursery – from Jackie Carey and Liam Whelan to Gary Kelly and Richard Dunne.

One of the club’s greatest claims to fame was that in the opening game of the 2023 women’s World Cup, two former Home Farm players were on the pitch, one for Ireland and one for Australia – in Abbie Larkin and Mary Fowler, who grew up for a few years in Dublin.

Ireland legends Dunne, Gary Kelly in his Leeds days and inset Jackie Carey, who captained Manchester United

While it was a schoolboy club nurturing young talent that Home Farm fostered its reputation, it was elected to the League of Ireland in 1972 and three years later achieved its greatest ever success as, in an underdog story to rival Leicester winning the Premier League, they won the FAI Cup.

Menton can still list off the names of all the players for the club’s most famous day in April 1975, including a young Dermot Keely who was in the centre of defence, and Martin Murray, who at 16 was the youngest player to win a FAI Cup medal.

‘Everyone but Jack Dempsey, who was in his late 20s or 30 at the time, was 24 years of age or under. The average age of the team was just 21 and a lot of the players were younger than that, it was an incredible achievement at the time,’ he says.

It is that sort of rich and illustrious history that Whelan, Honohan and the other stakeholders want to tap into when they were looking for a pathway back into the league. Home Farm, who had an association with Everton in the latter part of the 1990s, dropped out of the league in 1999 with the franchise being taken up by Dublin City who were eventually subsumed into Sporting Fingal, both now sadly defunct.

The Everton connection came through Martin Murray and saw one of the later graduates of the schoolboy club, Richard Dunne, whose uncle Theo was a coach at Home Farm, go over to Goodison Park as a teenager.

‘I played my schoolboy football at Home Farm and got picked up to go to Everton at 15,’ Dunne remembers.

‘We didn’t have the pathway produced by the National League then. And Home Farm was considered the top schoolboy club in Dublin at the time and when scouts and English clubs came over, this was the first port of call. That’s something that probably faded away over time, but hopefully, we can get it back.’

Team captain Jack Dempsey lifted the FAI Cup for Home Farm back in 1975

There are around 30 teams at the club now, 10 of them in an underage girls section. The hope is that the likes of Larkin and Fowler can be an inspiration for the next generation.

The club will also move to a new facility in the AUL next summer, as part of the deal that was made when the construction of the Metrolink means that they have to relocate temporarily from their nursery’s home on Mobhi Road in Glasnevin.

They have also got a tie-in with neighbouring Dublin City University, links that the club will hope to deepen. The third-level institution is seen more as a GAA university, but the hope is that they can develop a soccer scholarship programme, so players from the north of the city don’t have to travel to UCD or Shamrock Rovers.

Whelan, who availed of the UCD scholarship, says it is still in the early stages, but it is one aspect that reveals the ambitions of the club.

Nicola Brannigan, who formerly worked in the FAI marketing department but is now chief executive of the club, says the relationship has developed through the inaugural season in the national league.

‘We have students from DCU doing work experience at the club, we have communications students coming in to help us with social media, there is a law student from DCU, so that is one way that the relationship has worked. And then we have a few students or DCU graduates playing for the team,’ she says.

Under former Sligo Rovers star Gavin Peers, who played with the club as a youngster, the senior team have performed above themselves at times this season, but the ambitions are such they always felt they would be in contention to win the inaugural National League.

But the season has more being about putting Home Farm back on the map. Whelan knows from personal experience what can happen when clubs in the league endure harsh times.

Having scored in the FAI Cup final for Drogheda and winning a league title with them, he was there when things went awry a couple of years later.

Home Farm have not beaten Lucan United so far this season

‘There was a lot of good people in Drogheda at the time, but it is what can happen when the economy goes south for a club and that is why what we want to build here, we want to do in a conservative and sustainable way and it is why we made sure that the senior club, and the club that we want to eventually get back in the Premier Division, is separate from the schoolboy section.’

Whelan’s youngest son Sonny is now playing at the under-eight team, the second in a fourth generation of Whelans to pass through Home Farm, stretching back to Whelan’s father Paul and uncle Ronnie and his grandfather, Ronnie senior.

But a greater claim to fame was that Whelan’s goal for Drogheda in 2005 meant that he, his father Paul, who won it with Bohemians, and his grandfather Ronnie senior were the first three generations of the same family  to win a national cup in a European league.

But it all started in Home Farm, which is why he wants to bring the club back to the big-time, especially with the club's centenary coming up in 2028.

‘We want to bring back Home Farm, by using the foundations of what made the club in the past, and its rich history,’ he says.

‘This is where I learned manners, learned discipline, learned teamwork and all of that. The club always had the right ethos and this was just a case of leaving a legacy, showing what the club is and leaving it in a better place.’

Even though there is no promotion into the First Division this season, it feels like winning the inaugural National League will serve notice of the club’s intention of returning to where they feel they belong.

#1014. Preparing for 45C: How Germany tests its crisis response

A record heat wave. Five years of drought. A nation under pressure. Germany is running its biggest joint crisis exercise to date to test how authorities would cope with an escalating climate emergency.

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

It is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

The first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

Since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

At that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, said additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

"Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler said. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity."

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

"We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," said Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," said BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

This year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," said Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," said Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

A preliminary report with the main findings and respective recommendations is due to be published in the first quarter of next year. A full evaluation report will then be released later in the third quarter of 2027.

#1012. Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck

Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive markets.

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

#1011. Martin O'Neill's team selections in Europa League say it all about Celtic's glaring lack of ambition

Published: 13:07 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 16:44 EST, 27 November 2026

Ross Desmond started it at last season’s comedy turn of a Celtic AGM when more or less admitting that finances mean it’s time to run up the white flag when trying to compete in Europe.

And manager Martin O’Neill’s team selections in this term’s Europa League only heighten the concern that addressing a truly horrific record in UEFA competition dating back two decades now is not a priority.

It is a desperate situation for the club to be in. O’Neill might talk about rotation or private masterplans over impact substitutions, but it is seriously wrong that Camilo Duran, for example, was left on the bench for the recent meetings with Besiktas and Torreense.

Duran, himself, proved it by coming on and scoring the goals that mean qualification for the knockout rounds remains a distinct possibility despite everything.

It just looks like the club and its manager don’t really care all that much about Europe – or don’t see it as a key priority – and that’s not acceptable when they have charged their punters big-money for packages to get into the ground to watch it.

There are a number of things that need addressed when this year’s AGM rolls back around next Tuesday, though, and it is to be hoped punters and shareholders – probably the same thing, really – have prepared with cooler heads this time round.

Celtic line up for their tie against Torreense, with star man Camilo Duran again left on the bench

Last year became embarrassing, really, with people holding up red cards, jeering, walking out and chanting ‘Sack The Board’. They gave those at the top table the opportunity to bring the meeting to a halt and that’s exactly what happened before they had been properly challenged.

That behaviour is OK when making a point inside the stadium on matchday. If you want to win an argument – or unpick one – inside a business meeting, though, the shouting has to be replaced with clear thinking, planning and strong cases delivered in a coherent manner.

There are so many things to tear into CEO Michael Nicholson and co over. There’s the evident lack of long-term planning that has a 74-year-old in O’Neill still in charge of running the team.

There’s recruitment, in the week of a tie-up with little-known Pluto Data Analytics. Celtic went into their Champions League play-off with LASK Linz unprepared and suffered humiliation. Their dealings at the end of the summer window were erratic and scattergun.

Even marquee signings Kasper Hogh and Haissem Hassan are unravelling. They look like two guys totally unsuited to the way O’Neill wants to play and speak to a disjointed, failing policy.

There has been no full-time chairman appointed to replace 77-year-old interim Brian Wilson. There’s no sporting director or head of football operations. No one seems to want to explain who exactly will be working with Pluto to try and improve the club’s record on signings.

Martin O'Neill and assistant Shaun Maloney watch as Celtic toil against Torreense in Leiria

Parkhead’s now old and outdated. Millions lie around in the bank for no particular reason. Communication between the board and a disgruntled fanbase needs improved dramatically.

There is a lot to get through next week. That’s why there can be no place for student politics, silly protests, angry chanting. This board needs taken to task and it is to be hoped there are fans ready to step up to the mic and confront them calmly.

Celtic regard themselves as one of the biggest clubs in the world. This apparent insouciance over Europe is at complete odds with that, though.

It is as clear a sign as any that standards have slipped so badly at the champions and it is something that needs to be called out and challenged in the right way.

Robots compete in a football event during RoboCup 2026, a robotics and AI competition held at the Songdo Convensia convention centre in Incheon, South Korea. Credit: Ahn Young-joon/Associated Press/ALAMY

More than half of the world’s population now lives in cities, and that figure is projected to increase to nearly 70% by 2050. With the numbers of urban dwellers set to expand rapidly in some regions, a new generation of towns and cities is on the rise: communities that are designed to be cleaner and more efficient, driven by a host of technologies such as artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things — a network of sensors and devices that collect and transmit data about their surroundings.

As the global competition for talent and investment intensifies, many governments see these new cities and urban areas as strategic resources for boosting their innovative and economic competitiveness. Research facilities, both public and private, are central to this strategy.

In Songdo, South Korea — an early experiment in building a smart city from the ground up — biopharmaceutical giants such as Samsung Biologics have built major manufacturing facilities, and academic institutions such as Yonsei University have set up training and research centres to nurture scientists. In Hengqin, a rapidly developing district in the Pearl River Delta of southern China, research institutions also play a key role in a government strategy aimed at attracting talent, diversifying the economy and building a reputation for high-tech innovation.

For some researchers, purpose-built tech-centric cities provide them with the ideal environment to conduct experiments. Air-quality and traffic-flow research benefits greatly from consistent, real-time data gathered from many different locations, for instance. “Smart cities can offer something very valuable: a real-world laboratory,” says Dakota McCarty, a researcher of urban planning at George Mason University’s Songdo campus.

But building a liveable city from scratch takes more than implementing advanced technologies and creating favourable conditions for institutions. Many large-scale urban projects across the world are facing a collective challenge: how to convince talented people to live there?

The term ‘smart cities’ generally refers to places that are made to run more efficiently and sustainably through the extensive use of digital technologies. Songdo, located about 40 kilometres southwest of South Korea’s capital, Seoul, is often described as “the world’s first smart city”1. The idea for Songdo dates back to the 1980s, but construction did not begin until several years after the 1998 Asian financial crisis, when the Incheon metropolitan government proposed developing Songdo as part of a free economic zone aimed at attracting foreign investment2. Today, Songdo spans about 5,260 hectares of coastal land, roughly the size of Manhattan.

In 2011, a series of futuristic technologies was built into Songdo’s infrastructure as part of South Korea’s campaign to establish ‘ubiquitous cities’, its name for smart cities at the time. One example is its underground waste-collection system — a network of subterranean pipes that suck rubbish directly from individual households, rather than transporting it by road. The system uses bins fitted with sensors and built into the stairwells of residential buildings. Once the sensors detect that the bins are full, the system will automatically empty them and send the rubbish through the pipes to a waste centre. Recyclable rubbish is cleaned and reused, and food waste is processed into compost.

In addition to the use of sensors in waste disposal, Songdo has deployed thousands of sensors to help manage other city functions such as traffic and security. These sensor networks link to a control centre run by the Incheon Free Economic Zone Authority (IFEZA), which manages Songdo and two other free economic zones in Incheon.

Extensive sensor networks and integrated data systems are a major asset for Songdo’s researchers and students, says McCarty, who moved from the United States to South Korea nearly a decade ago and has spent the past three years in Songdo. “In a place like Songdo, which was planned from the start with smart infrastructure, and has universities, industry and public agencies relatively close together, there is much more potential to test ideas in real urban conditions,” he says.

Data can be accessed through a website run by IFEZA, with additional data sets available on request. McCarty and his students are combining traffic data obtained from IFEZA with observations collected on the ground to build a model of Songdo’s walkability. The team hopes to show that adjusting traffic-light timings could make the city more accommodating for pedestrians without increasing congestion3.

There is a downside to building a city’s renown around cutting-edge technology, however: other cities can catch up. As the novelty of Songdo’s original smart-city infrastructure started to fade, it increasingly sought to build its identity around industry clusters that are harder for competitors to replicate.

Biopharmaceuticals, for example, is a strategic industry for South Korea, with the government committing US$1.5 billion to support the sector over this decade. Celltrion, one of South Korea’s largest biotechnology companies, was among the first firms of its kind to commit to Songdo in 2003. Samsung Biologics, a major biopharmaceutical manufacturer, established its headquarters there in 2011.

Moves like this helped to create a new development path for the city, says Sohyun Park, a researcher of economic geography at George Mason University in Songdo. “As these firms expanded, local and national governments increasingly concentrated resources on developing Songdo as a biotechnology cluster,” says Park. As of 2021, Songdo was home to around 60 biotechnology companies, and the government’s plan is to expand that number to 700 by 2030.

Dakota McCarty and his team at George Mason University’s Songdo campus are using traffic data to come up with ways to make the city more pedestrian-friendly.Credit: Dakota McCarty / George Mason University Korea

Such expansion depends on the support of Songdo’s university sector to train a new generation of biomedical talent. Yonsei University, which has its main campus in Seoul and an international campus in Songdo, opened the Korean National Institute for Bioprocessing Research and Training (K-NIBRT) in Songdo last year. The project has received around 60.9 billion South Korean won (US$41 million) from national and regional authorities and aims to train 2,000 biopharmaceutical specialists each year to address labour shortages locally and across the country.

K-NIBRT benefits from Songdo’s complete biopharmaceuticals value chain, says Gyoonhee Han, the institution’s director-general, because its research institutes, drug manufacturers and raw material and equipment suppliers are all conveniently packed into a radius of a 10-minute drive. This tight-knit ecosystem means that companies, researchers and academics can collaborate efficiently where industry is located, and trainees are able to enter the workforce as soon as they graduate, says Han.

Beyond biopharmaceuticals, Songdo plans on expanding its university base more broadly, particularly within its Incheon Global Campus (IGC), a higher-education zone established in the early 2010s and backed by US$1 billion in investment from the Korean and Incheon Metropolitan City governments. Campuses of three US universities — George Mason University, the University of Utah and the State University of New York (which has two Songdo campuses) — plus Belgium’s Ghent University have opened in the IGC, and six more universities are expected to join in the coming years.

Songdo’s evolution reflects a broader challenge for smart-city projects: advanced technologies and digital infrastructure can attract investment and attention, but long-term R&D activity depends on assets that are harder to build: universities, skilled workforces and specialized industry clusters.

In Hengqin, an island in southern China’s Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), regional and central governments are trying to combine both approaches. In addition to the autonomous-vehicle technologies that Hengqin and the wider GBA area are known for — including driverless buses, taxis and delivery services — universities and research institutes are being positioned at the centre of Hengqin’s development strategy.

Hengqin entered a new phase of cross-border cooperation in 2009, when China’s central government passed legislation enabling Macau, a special administrative region with its own governance system, to exercise jurisdiction over part of the neighbouring island. The goal was to allow the University of Macau to move its campus away from a densely populated casino hub, and more broadly to have Hengqin serve as a bridge between Macau and the neighbouring Guangdong province.

These efforts were accelerated in 2021, when China established the Guangdong–Macao In-Depth Cooperation Zone — an economic and administrative area covering more than 100 km2 of Hengqin, run jointly by the Macau and Guangdong governments. One of the biggest projects within this new zone is an international university town, expected to be completed by 2030 at a cost of nearly 20 billion Macau pataca (US$2.47 billion). At least three universities plan to open campuses there — the University of Macau (which will build an additional campus alongside an existing one), Macao Polytech University and Macao University of Tourism — to accommodate roughly 20,000 students.

Students develop flexible electronics in the Soft Sensors-Actuators-Robots Laboratory at the University of Macau’s main campus in Hengqin.Credit: The University of Macau

“Academic and research capabilities are essential, because they provide the talent, knowledge and innovation infrastructure that Hengqin needs to become a science and technology hub,” says Yonghua Song, president of the Macao Association for Higher Education Development and rector of the University of Macau. Song adds that new facilities such as the University of Macau’s Faculty of Information Science and Computing, opened in August, are expected to train talent in highly competitive areas such as artificial intelligence, microelectronics and financial technology.

Like Songdo, researchers in Hengqin benefit from its extensive smart-city infrastructure, including the large networks of sensors in operation across the island. According to Ma Shaodan, a wireless-communications researcher at the University of Macau’s State Key Laboratory of Internet of Things for Smart City in Hengqin, having smart-city infrastructure right outside the laboratory removes many of the constraints of conventional research environments. “It provides an invaluable physical context that accelerates our research, strengthens our regional impact, and serves as a tangible blueprint to inspire the next generation of engineers,” she says.

Early signs suggest that Hengqin’s strategy to become a place of high-tech innovation is gaining momentum: the University of Macau has expanded its presence, research infrastructure has proliferated and authorities continue to invest heavily in the cooperation zone.

#1005. The Preview: Scottish Cup is the perfect proving ground for Clydebank and Co., as band of Lowland League clubs look to make their mark

Published: 15:17 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 16:44 EST, 27 November 2026

If Clydebank aren’t careful, getting the better of SPFL opposition will soon become something of an expectation rather than a hope. Then again, given their lofty ambitions, that’s exactly the kind of club they want to be.

It’s been 23 extraordinary years since its reformation, having gone bust following a series of events which left one of Scottish football’s great clubs — and great communities, for that matter — on its knees.

That it has taken less than a quarter of a century to get back within touching distance of the SPFL frankly beggars’ belief.

Win the Lowland League West — they currently sit three points behind leaders Largs Thistle with a couple of games in hand — and they will have a crack at earning promotion to the big time via a play-off.

Yet, as exciting a prospect as that may be, it’s something which will be a million miles from the minds of the players, staff and supporters as they rock up at Holm Park this afternoon for a Scottish Cup third-round clash against Championship high-flyers Livingston.

This, of course, is not uncharted territory. Indeed, it’s the third time in as many years that the club have made it to this stage of the competition, and even made it one round further in 2024-25 before bowing out to Hibs at Easter Road.

Clydebank will welcome Championship side Livingston to Holm Park tomorrow

Yet it wouldn’t necessarily be a great surprise if they were to reach that stage again this time around given the way in which they’ve gone about their business with such professionalism against teams playing much higher up in the football pyramid.

Their incredible run to the KDM Evolution Trophy quarter-finals saw them defeat Dumbarton, East Fife, Kelty Hearts and Alloa Athletic before progressing on penalties against Queen’s Park on Tuesday night.

That win marked the 77th consecutive domestic match in which Clydebank have found the net, incidentally, having surpassed Celtic’s record of 75 set in 2017 a few days earlier.

Pulling off a shock once, maybe even twice, could be put down to luck. To do so habitually is something different. Which is why this is a bit of a nightmare draw for Livi.

The days of non-league clubs simply making up the numbers at this point of the competition are a thing of the past, with the gap between the second and fifth tiers of Scottish football seemingly getting smaller with each passing year.

That the likes of Clydebank will genuinely believe they can beat a team chasing an immediate return to the top flight suggests as much.

They are not the only Lowland League West side in action today, with Cumnock Juniors eyeing up a shock as they welcome Championship outfit Arbroath, who know a thing or two about upsetting the odds having punched well above their weight for long enough.

You suspect Raith Rovers won’t be relishing their journey to face Troon at Portland Park, a stadium perhaps best known for hosting a few Brazilian chaps including Pele, Garrincha, Tostao and Zico ahead of the 1966 World Cup in England.

The Lowland League West side have beaten the likes of Alloa and Queen's Park this season

The names of today’s visitors may not quite carry the same gravitas, but nevertheless, it’s arguably the biggest game in Troon’s 80-year history.

One thing is for certain: there will be at least one Lowland League West club in the hat for the next round, with Renfrew — who have Argyll McCoist, son of Rangers legend Ally in their squad — going head-to-head with Cumbernauld Colts, with both chasing a money-spinning fourth-round tie against one of the country’s big guns.

Bo’ness United and Brechin City — both battling it out in the Lowland League East this season — are in the same boat ahead of their meeting at Newtown Park.

Fifty miles separate Ross County and Brora Rangers ahead of their clash in Dingwall, but in Highland terms, it constitutes something of a derby.

The visitors are looking to follow in their opponents footsteps by getting up to the SPFL this season, 22 years after County broke through. And they are going about it the right way too, having gone unbeaten in the Highland League so far this term.

Funnily enough, they are coming against the only other team in Scotland’s top five tiers who share that particular accolade.

And those in charge at Morton will be praying their side can survive their trip to League Two’s basement side Annan Athletic in the hope of pulling a lucrative fixture in the next round.

Amid all the financial uncertainty and concern regarding the future of the Cappielow club these days — even more so following the news earlier this week that main sponsor Dalrada Technology Ltd has been placed in liquidation — goodness knows they need some positivity around the place.

#1004. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.
