#956. Liverpool Confidential squad audit: The NINE stars who could leave Anfield, the latest on each of their futures and what Reds should do with them

Published: 12:00 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 12:08 EST, 26 November 2026

Liverpool's dressing room has felt like a revolving door of uncertainty in the last five years, with constant doubt about certain players’ futures.

Even when the team won the Premier League title two seasons ago, there was a never-ending subplot about the futures of Mohamed Salah, Virgil van Dijk and Trent Alexander-Arnold.

Now there is ambiguity over Van Dijk again, plus Alisson, Alexis Mac Allister and others, with the depth of Liverpool's squad still an issue to be addressed.

In this week’s Liverpool Confidential, we take a look at all nine players with uncertain futures, reveal what we are hearing about them, and reach a verdict on what we would do if we were sporting director Julian Ward.

The situation: The 35-year-old club legend's contract runs out at the end of this season, so from January 1 he would be able to sign a pre-contract with an overseas club to join them in the summer.

Owners Fenway Sports Group have a long-standing unwritten policy not to offer big deals to players over the age of 30, which led to the likes of Gini Wijnaldum and Andy Robertson leaving on free transfers. But they broke this rule two years ago to offer Van Dijk a new deal. Will they do it again?

Liverpool's owners FSG broke their rule on offering 30-somethings big deals two years ago to tie down Virgil van Dijk. They should do it again

What we’re hearing: Van Dijk would be more than open to staying. Sources in Italy say AC Milan have approached him over moving there – but whether he would want to is a completely different story.

Van Dijk is yet to be offered a new deal at Liverpool but this is not a reason for fans to panic. They always bide their time with these things.

Liverpool are carefully managing Van Dijk’s workload for the first time, as evidenced by him being a substitute in Bruges this week. The squad have had a day off on Thursday ahead of returning to training on Friday for the Merseyside derby.

Our verdict: There is a narrative that Van Dijk is starting to show his age. Maybe he is not quite at the extraordinarily high level he maintained in previous years but the skipper is still integral to everything the Reds do. If the two parties can agree on a one-year extension, it would suit everyone. But the Reds must also prepare for life without the formidable Dutchman, whenever that actually happens.

The situation: See above. Alisson is also out of contract at the end of the season after the club triggered a one-year extension last summer.

What we’re hearing: The Brazilian wants to stay and is in talks to do so. There are murmurs that he could ask for a big financial package.

Our verdict: Alisson is still in the top three goalkeepers in the Premier League. Like Van Dijk, a short extension might suit everyone.

Liverpool are well stocked in the goalkeeper department, with the club believing Giorgi Mamardashvili is better than he has shown so far. They will soon welcome Belgian 18-year-old Lucca Brughmans, who is rated as one of the best up-and-coming keepers in the game.

But are they better than Alisson right now? No.

Alisson wants to stay and remains one of the top three goalkeepers in the Premier League

The situation: The Argentine has publicly declared he feels let down by the club after he was informed they would not yet extend his contract, and the 27-year-old's deal also runs out at the end of next season.

What we’re hearing: His father and agent Carlos Mac Allister is expecting to hold talks with Liverpool in the coming weeks to set out his demands and may reach a compromise.

Our verdict: Mac Allister has been Liverpool’s best midfielder this season. He has been so good, in fact, that the club should rethink their stance, which they may do with Ward now installed as sporting director.

But there are still 18 months until his deal expires. What if his form falls off a cliff again as it did last season? No one was desperate for a new deal then. Liverpool should bide their time.

Alexis Mac Allister has been Liverpool’s best midfielder this season and, as it stands, deserves a new contract. But why would Liverpool rush into a decision?

The situation: Out of contract in the summer after what will be 12 years at the club.

What we’re hearing: Gomez is still enjoying life at Liverpool despite not being a regular starter. He will turn 30 in the summer so it is hard to see him being handed a new deal.

Our verdict: The defender is loved by all at the club as the longest-serving player and there is a sadness that injuries have held his career back to a degree. But it feels like this summer would be the right time to move on.

He came close in summer 2024 when he was left out of the first matchday squad of the Arne Slot era, and again in 2025 when Marc Guehi was inches away from signing for Liverpool.

It feels like next summer is the right time for Joe Gomez to move on after over a decade at the club

The situation: Out of contract in the summer after returning from an unsuccessful loan at Roma last season.

What we’re hearing: You don't need to be a mind-reader to know what the recruitment team are thinking here: Liverpool’s full back department is the weakest area of the squad, especially at left back with neither Tsimikas nor Milos Kerkez impressing this season.

Our verdict: Tsimikas seems a well-liked member of the dressing room and will always be remembered for big moments such as his winning penalty in the 2022 FA Cup final shootout – but the Greek international falls short of Liverpool’s level. A new left back must be on the shopping list.

Kostas Tsimikas seems a well-liked member of the dressing room and will always be remembered for big moments, but the Greek international falls short of Liverpool’s level

The situation: The Dutch wing-back has not hit the required level on a consistent basis since joining Liverpool from Bayer Leverkusen for £29.5million last year.

What we’re hearing: There have been reports linking him with a move to Saudi Arabia, but Frimpong has just returned from another injury lay-off and is determined to settle at Liverpool and impress Iraola, who likes attack-minded full backs.

Our verdict: Give him until the end of the season at least. There were glimpses of form last season over the Christmas period. Frimpong does not seem to fit the current system but, given his injuries, he has never really had a chance to prove people wrong.

Jeremie Frimpong is determined to settle at Liverpool and impress Andoni Iraola, who likes attack-minded full backs

The situation: On loan from Barcelona but Liverpool have an option to sign the 27-year-old Uruguayan for around £47m.

What we’re hearing: No decisions are being made just yet but Liverpool are delighted with the impact made by fan favourite Araujo, and he is loving life in England. Liverpool retain the right to renegotiate and pay less than the pre-agreed fee.

Our verdict: Araujo's leadership, experience and versatility are all huge bonuses. He has been outstanding at both right back and centre half, and it seems like an obvious decision to make the move permanent. Put the money on the table.

Liverpool are delighted with the impact made by fan favourite Ronald Araujo, and he is loving life in England

The situation: The 33-year-old has not played a single minute under Andoni Iraola, and it is now nine months since his last Liverpool appearance – in a 1-0 win at Sunderland in February. He was excluded from the Champions League squad for the group phase.

What we’re hearing: Endo has never kicked up a fuss but will be keen for game time at this point of his career.

Our verdict: The Japan captain signed as a stop-gap in 2023 and he played an underrated role in the title triumph as a substitute that helped see out games. He played on through injury in that match at Sunderland last season – his only league start of the campaign – and should be given a warm farewell, though a January exit suits everyone.

Wataru Endo has never kicked up a fuss but will be keen for game time at this point of his career

Federico Chiesa has rarely been fit while at Liverpool and it feels like it is in everyone’s best interests for the Italian to move on

The situation: The 51-cap Italy winger is not in Liverpool’s Champions League squad and young players like Lewis Koumas and Jayden Danns are ahead of him in the pecking order. The 29-year-old has had just two minutes of competitive action this season.

What we’re hearing: There is a constant background noise of ‘Italian clubs are circling for Chiesa’. An exit seems likely in January, though Chiesa has come close to leaving several times before now and not done so.

Our verdict: Chiesa and Liverpool has just not worked out, despite the Italian becoming a bit of a cult hero last year thanks to some late winners off the bench. He has rarely been fully fit and it feels like it is in everyone’s best interests for the Italian to move on.

#955. Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?

The heat is on Australia as chief negotiator at the COP31 UN climate conference to forge a path away from coal and gas, and to protect Pacific neighbors facing rising sea levels.

In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.

The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.

"These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation."

Yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet committed to phasing them out.

As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

Australia is home to 56% of the world's coal mine projects currently in the pipeline, notes environmental nonprofit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.

"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," said Melanie Pill, founder of The Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.

The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.

"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbors, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales.

As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, said Pill.

This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," said Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He noted that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," said Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

In 2025, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions."

The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit road map.

But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region, from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Australia must commit to "substantial new funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said his colleague Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption, with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.

"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," said Houlie.

#954. When is the Nations League quarter-final draw?

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

The remaining dates for the Nations League are:

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June

#953. Swansea investigate after naked image of player is shared on social media ahead of grudge match with bitter rivals Cardiff

Published: 12:15 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 14:05 EST, 26 November 2026

Swansea City have launched an internal investigation after an inappropriate image of one of its players was shared on social media.

The image, which emerged on X, formerly Twitter, on Wednesday night, appeared to show a Swansea City player naked standing beside a bed.

The photo, first taken on Snapchat, has since disappeared online after violating the social media site’s rules.

A Swansea City spokesperson confirmed to Daily Mail Sport that the club are investigating the photo internally but no further comment will be made at this time.

The photo, which was first shared by a Cardiff City fan, has emerged just days before this Sunday’s South Wales derby between Swansea and Cardiff, with tensions between both fanbases high now that they are back in the same division.

Swansea City have launched an internal investigation after an inappropriate image of one of its players was shared on social media

While Swansea plan to speak to the player to establish the key facts behind the image, there is also a legal side that cannot be ignored.

In England and Wales it is a criminal offence to share naked or intimate photos without consent under Section 66B of the Sexual Offences Act 2003.

Should an investigation determine the image has been tampered with, including AI-generated or manipulated 'deepfakes,' which was one of the allegations on social media on Wednesday night, that too is a criminal act under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.

#952. Whiff of arrogance as Arsenal unexpectedly implode

Arsenal were cruising. This was life on Premier League easy street, but from complete control of this game against Newcastle United, they tossed it away. It was a spectacular, unexpected implosion. They were extremely fortunate to escape with a point.

You cannot switch off away from home in the Premier League and you certainly can never be complacent against a team with Newcastle’s home crowd behind them.

From control to disarray. From looking like champions, Arsenal, who also lost goalkeeper David Raya to a worrying looking injury, rumbled under pressure. To go from dominance to being grateful for a draw, this was a flaky side of the Premier League leaders we have not seen for a while.

“We have lost two points,” said manager Mikel Arteta. “We were exceptional in the first half, the intensity and the quality, we should have been two, three or four goals up.

“When you don’t do that, in the second half you cannot give the opposition belief and you cannot give them goals. We did both. We started to lose duels, second balls, we gave it away.”

Was it arrogance? Did the title-holders start to believe they were simply too good to be hurt or worried by a team with Newcastle’s obvious limitations? It looked like it. The way Arsenal fell apart as soon as the momentum in the game shifted in the home team’s favour in the second half was shocking.

Newcastle were dreadful before the break and managed just one attack before half-time. Perhaps it was all too easy for Arteta’s side. They have become used to ferocious battles on Tyneside, but this was a stroll for 45 minutes. When it turned into a proper test after half-time, though, they folded.

"Absolutely clinical!" Eberechi Eze scores his first Premier League goal of the season to give Arsenal the lead 🔴 https://t.co/34IbZuuJuN

The visitors took a deserved lead, through Eberechi Eze, having barely had to break sweat, but the way they approached the second half was baffling. As soon as Newcastle got in their faces and made it a scrap, Arsenal were bullied, ruffled and rushed into mistakes.

To give the opposition one goal against the run of play can be forgiven, but to do it a second time, when the heat is cranked up, hints at a fragility we no longer thought existed under Arteta.

The first goal came from a blunder by captain Martin Odegaard. It was a lazy, sloppy swing of the leg to try to clear a throw-in and the ball sliced backwards. When it looped into the path of Will Osula, he squared to the unmarked Harvey Barnes who put away the equaliser comfortably.

"Horrendous error!" Harvey Barnes puts Newcastle level 👊 https://t.co/YWrHZPxBIo

It was Newcastle’s first shot on target, but Arsenal’s air of invincibility vanished and the crowd sensed it. Newcastle players responded to the noise, snapping into tackles and pouring forward in numbers, yet the second goal was also an Arsenal gift.

How do you leave the giant Dan Burn unmarked at a corner? Newcastle’s captain had so much time and space the crowd were able to scream in anticipation before his header flew goalwards, eventually bundled across the line by his centre-back colleague Malick Thiaw.

Malick Thiaw is in the right place to fire it in and give Newcastle the lead against Arsenal! 🔥 https://t.co/nthaH3aOJD

Newcastle deserved it. For half an hour in the second half they were the better side. From the depths of despair, from the apathy and boos of half-time, this was a completely different team.

If this is the vertical football Matthias Jaissle has preached since he arrived in August, Newcastle supporters can buy into it. There was speed, a physicality and a boldness in this second-half performance. It was fun and exciting. It was football played on the front foot. It was what we were promised when the German replaced Eddie Howe.

“That is Newcastle’s DNA, the second half is what we want this team to play like,” said Jaissle. “We knew there would be ups and downs this season, but if we can put that performance together for 90 minutes we can definitely say we are moving in the right direction.”

The problem is, Newcastle have not put a 90-minute performance like this together all season. We have only seen it in flashes and as good as the second half was, we cannot lose sight of the fact the first was abject. Newcastle’s football was aimless, clueless and dysfunctional. One attack before the break, one deflected shot wide is simply not good enough.

The transformation at half-time was unexpected. The substitutes helped; Tino Livramento was a massive upgrade on Amar Dedic at right-back, Jacob Ramsey improved the midfield and Anthony Elanga brought speed and, yes, a vertical threat to their attack.

But Jaissle’s side did not hold on for the win. They had the chances to score a third, but it was their ambition to do so that caused their downfall. Arsenal’s class shone again, passing through the lines to release Noni Madueke.

The winger still had lots to do, but having cut inside, leaving two Newcastle defenders on the ground, his shot squeezed through a crowd and through the arms of goalkeeper Lukasz Hornicek. The Czech international will not want to see it again, and this comes after a similar mistake in the home defeat to Everton.

Noni Madueke equalises for Arsenal! 💥 https://t.co/VNXOoNDxiJ

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Arsenal boss said: “My feeling is that we lost two points today. I think we were exceptional in the first half. At every level. Our intensity, the clarity that we have, how to attack the jumps of Newcastle every time they wanted to go man-to-man, the composure that we have, the way we use our relationship to break their press. And it should have been 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0 up, clear.

“But it wasn’t. And when it wasn’t, then we expected in the second half that we have to again raise the level because the opponent is going to have a reaction. And the opponent did have a reaction and we were very below the level that is required to stretch the gap in a game like this in this stadium. And then we gave them belief.

“And I say we give them belief because we give them a goal, we give them a throw-in that we just give them the ball. We have no structure to control the opposite winger. We concede a goal and it’s game on. And from that it became a very chaotic game. Every set-piece, we know that they are exceptional at it and we concede from a set piece.

“And then you have to react. And then we went back to the team that the exceptional team that we were in the first half again for another 25 minutes and we scored a great goal. We create infinity of openings to create and score the third goal, but we lack some time or to be precise, to make that count.”

"We've got the quality." Harvey Barnes is hoping Newcastle can build on the performance against Arsenal and find some consistency this season 🧱 https://t.co/hWvVLyJrIW

"I reckon 2-2 was a fair result." Noni Madueke reflects on Arsenal's performance against Newcastle at St James' Park 🔴 https://t.co/UfDi5SGgat

"That is the one player that is irreplaceable in that team." Jamie Redknapp says David Raya going off injured is a massive blow for Arsenal 🔊 https://t.co/JZ1ABfH2RM

"It was a bit worrying to see Arsenal collapse like they did" Ian Wright shares his full-time thoughts as Arsenal draw 2-2 with Newcastle at St James' Park 💭 https://t.co/Z8olpBf9q4

"He made three great changes!" 🤩 Jamie Redknapp discusses Newcastle's huge improvement in the second half 💪 https://t.co/izwzxgE45R

A brave second-half display earns Newcastle a well-deserved draw against Arsenal. After falling behind to Eze’s 33rd-minute opener, Jaissle made a triple change at the break that completely transformed the hosts, who scored twice through Barnes and Thiaw. However, Arsenal fought back and levelled thanks to Madueke as both sides had to settle for a draw. Arsenal drop points for just the second time in 11 league matches this season and stay top, while Newcastle remain 12th.

It finishes level at St. James' Park 🤝 https://t.co/jwFfknJKxh

Gyokeres darts inside of Livramento to work a yard of space, but whips a powerful effort over the bar. He claims Arsenal should have a corner, but the referee rules that it’s a goal kick. Time is rapidly running out for both sides to score a late winner.

Arteta is searching for a hero and orders a late double attacking change in stoppage time. Merino and Gyokeres are on for Havertz and Odegaard.

Hall was at fault for Arsenal’s opener but has been brilliant in the second half. He slumps to the deck and hobbles off for Botman. It’s unclear whether it’s an injury or fatigue. Newcastle fans will pray it is the latter.

There will be nine minutes of added time. More drama is a definite possibility.

Arsenal are on top and piling the pressure on Newcastle as we approach the 90-minute mark. The hosts deserve something from this game based on their second-half display.

It’s end-to-end action at the moment, with both teams looking shaky at the back. It would not be at all surprising if either side found another goal.

Newcastle make a late attacking change as Wissa replaces Willock. Can he help his side find a late winner?

Burn catches Timber with a late, sliding tackle in the corner as the Arsenal man goes to cross. The Newcastle captain tells Timber to get up and Madueke rushes over to defend his teammate before he and Burn start pushing each other. Both players are carded for that flashpoint and Arsenal take a free kick, which Hornicek catches comfortably.

It’s brilliant build-up from the league leaders. Havertz and Odegaard combine, with the latter playing in Madueke. The Arsenal winger cuts inside a couple of desperate Newcastle challengers before squeezing a slightly deflected effort underneath Hornicek. The Newcastle goalkeeper should probably do better, but Arsenal have responded like champions. This game is so finely poised now.

Noni Madueke equalises for Arsenal! 💥 https://t.co/VNXOoNDxiJ

Miley darts into Arsenal’s penalty area after receiving Barnes’ pass. For a split-second, it looked like Rice was about to commit a last-man foul as he weighed up whether to pull Miley down, but Kepa rushes out to intercept and save his side on this occasion.

Newcastle fly forward again as Willock’s strong run and deflected shot earns the hosts a corner. From Hall’s delivery, Havertz inadvertently flicks the ball against his own crossbar. It’s wave after wave of Newcastle pressure.

Nobody saw this coming at half time. Arsenal were cruising and in complete control but they gifted Newcastle an equaliser through Martin Ødegaard’s sliced clearance and something stirred inside St James’ Park. The atmosphere completely shifted and the champions have wilted under a sudden wave of Newcastle pressure. Complacency is dangerous especially away at Newcastle. You do not leave Dan Burn unmarked at a corner. Arsenal have self destructed.

Confirmation of that triple change for Arsenal as Kepa, Lewis-Skelly and Tzolis replace Raya, Guimaraes and Eze. Unsurprisingly, Guimaraes was heavily booed as he departed.

Raya looks to be in serious discomfort and can’t continue as he walks off holding his arm. Kepa is ready to come on. This second half has been a disaster for Arsenal. It also looks like Tzolis and Lewis-Skelly are coming on.

Newcastle look like a completely different side in this second half. Credit to Jaissle, his triple half-time change has worked wonders. Surely Arteta must be considering some substitutions of his own soon. Raya is down again and seems to have an issue with his shoulder or arm.

Incredible scenes! No one saw this coming at half-time. Hall curls in a corner and Burn peels away from Timber at the back post. Raya does well to save the Newcastle captain’s unmarked header, but Thiaw reacts quickest to knock in the rebound from close range. The home players rush to the corner to celebrate in front of the jubilant Gallowgate End. The goal survives a VAR check and Newcastle’s lead is confirmed. What are Arsenal made of now?

Malick Thiaw is in the right place to fire it in and give Newcastle the lead against Arsenal! 🔥 https://t.co/nthaH3aOJD

Miley tries his luck from long range and arrows a strike at goal which is straight at Raya. It stings the palms of the Arsenal goalkeeper. Yet again, it’s another positive moment for Newcastle.

This game is getting more feisty as Barnes catches Konsa with the hosts springing a high press. The Newcastle goal-scorer is booked for the challenge.

Hall dispossesses Madueke and gallops down the wing. Rice can’t catch him and bumps into the back of the defender to earn himself a yellow card. Arsenal look slighly rattled in this second half.

There’s a break in the play at the start of this half as Willock accidentally collides with Raya and the Arsenal goalkeeper holds his head. The medical staff are on to treat him.

Another abject, clueless, and directionless performance from Newcastle United in front of their own supporters. Arsenal have dominated the game and have not had to get out of second gear. It is hard to see what Matthias Jaissle’s team is trying to do and patience is wearing thin.

Yes, of course, they are playing the best team in the country but the supporters are not stupid. They have seen this sort of performance far too many times already this season. The most damning thing you can say is that there is no excitement. Even the boos for Bruno are half-hearted.

Boos ring out on the half-time whistle from the home fans. It’s been complete and utter domination from Arsenal. Eze’s resounding finish separates the sides, but the visitors could easily be two or three goals ahead. Newcastle look clueless in possession and are yet to record a shot on target.

Hall makes a goal-saving block! On this occasion, he comes to Newcastle’s rescue. Odegaard rolls a pass into the onrushing Madueke, who makes a great run drifting in from the right wing. Hall tracks the Arsenal attacker and makes a brilliant sliding block to deny Madueke from close range.

Once again, Hall switches off and Madueke pounces on the defender’s mistake as he tries to let the ball travel out of play. Madueke keeps it in and leads an Arsenal attack, but from a tight angle and under pressure from the covering Thiaw, his shot is smothered by Hornicek.

Arsenal are cruising and we’re still waiting for Newcastle to wake up. The away side haven’t created loads of chances, but they’re in control and have limited the hosts to nearly zero attacking threat.

After zero goals in his first ten matches for club and country this season, Eberechi Eze has now scored three goals in his last eight appearances.

All the noise inside St James’ Park is coming from the travelling Arsenal fans. Newcastle look lost and are really struggling to fashion any patterns of play in possession.

It’s a clinical opener for the visitors and Eze has his first Premier League goal of the season. Hall fails to deal with Konsa’s long ball and Havertz steals possession from him. The German then slides a delightful reverse pass behind Dedic and through to Eze, who lets the ball run across his body before smashing a clinical one-on-one effort into the roof of the net. Arsenal are deservedly ahead and Newcastle have barely laid a glove on them.

St James’ Park was about to erupt, and not in a good way for the hosts! Arsenal are dominating possession and territory. Newcastle United are struggling to advance up the pitch, and once again, there still seems to be no real improvement in Jaissle’s “vertical football” approach.

After 23 minutes, Newcastle goalkeeper Lukás Hornícek has had 15 touches of the ball. Only Dan Burn and Lewis Hall have had more for Newcastle. The home side seem unable to work the ball forward at all. Seemingly every passage of possession results in a Newcastle player turning towards their own goal and shovelling it back to the keeper.

Safe to say that Hornicek does not look comfortable with the ball at his feet. Dedic passes back to him and under a little bit of pressure from Odegaard, he boots the ball straight out of play. From there, Arsenal fashion an attack as Timber strides forward and finds Havertz, who lashes a shot wide from a tight angle.

This game is yet to burst into life. It’s been a relatively measured start from both sides so far. Guimaraes has only had 12 touches so the boos have been limited to this point.

Murphy chops inside of Calafiori and smashes a shot at goal. It takes a massive deflection off Barnes, who was trying to get out of the way, but the ball flies just wide of Arsenal’s near post. Raya was worried for a second there as he frantically dived to make sure.

Hornicek is nearly embarrassed by Havertz as the Newcastle goalkeeper dawdles on the ball and takes too long to clear. The German forward closes in and blocks Hornicek’s kick, but luckily for the hosts, the ball spins away from goal towards Hall’s feet.

Arsenal go close early on. Murphy does well to barge past Guimaraes and then attempts a very ambitious lob over Raya from just inside Arsenal’s half. However, the Newcastle man’s hopeful effort skids very far off target. It would take a miracle to beat Raya from that range.

More than £300m worth of signings are on the Newcastle bench this evening and another £72m sitting in the stands. That points to some bungled recruitment decisions over the last 18 months.

The fact that neither Aladji Bamba nor Bazoumane Toure can even make the matchday squad after joining in the summer before Matthias Jaissle was appointed manager is also damning.

There could be some awkward conversations between Jaissle and sporting director Ross Wilson before the January transfer window.

Then again, it was Jaissle who pushed to sign Nico Gonzalez from Manchester City and was thrilled to sign Mathias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille. They cost just over £100m and both only  make the bench against  Arsenal.

St James’ Park is absolutely bouncing. Can Newcastle upset Arsenal’s rhythm and disrupt the runaway leaders’ winning run?

Loud boos and whistles from Newcastle fans when Bruno Guimraes’ name is announced in the Arsenal team and a huge cheer from the away fans.

#951. Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does "electrification" mean?

Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels. That is according to a recent analysis by the International Energy Agency, which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

But the way the electricity running these things is generated is also important. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.

Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.

Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.

It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.

In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

The World Resources Institute, an independent research organization, recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity and electrified demand.

According to the International Energy Agency, annual grid investment has to increase by about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (five to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (one to five years), and EV charging infrastructure (one to two years).

Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

#950. How Xabi Alonso's brittle Blues have wilted this season: KIERAN GILL runs the rule over all TWENTY Premier League goals conceded as new manager faces urgent demand to patch up leaky defence

Published: 17:33 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 17:33 EST, 26 November 2026

Bullied by Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey, then by Leeds United’s Dominic Calvert-Lewin. Liam Delap, of all people, is probably the last striker that Chelsea’s defenders want to be facing next.

A striker who is seen as something of a brutish throwback. A striker with a point to prove versus his old employers who were happy to sell him after a single season. A striker who will know, having trained with Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana, how to make this an uncomfortable match.

Delap will lead the line for Nottingham Forest, and as if Colwill and Co needed any additional spotlight on them, this Premier League encounter will take place on Friday under the lights of the City Ground – about as intimidating a setting as they could have asked for.

Chelsea have conceded 20 Premier League goals this season. It is as many as they have scored, and so as much as we applauded their attacking earlier this term, we must likewise scrutinise the defending to the same degree.

Daily Mail Sport watched back all 20 to analyse, see who was at fault and issue each a Keystone Cops rating. Yes, there have been some 10 out of 10s.

Chelsea have conceded 20 goals already in the Premier League after losing 4-1 at home to Leeds. Pictured: Noah Okafor scores Leeds first goal in their win at Stamford Bridge

Xabi Alonso's defence must be scrutinised over the nature of the goals they are conceding

1 – Fulham, Josh King, 23rd minute, for 1-1

Xabi Alonso’s first taste of a setback on day one. All King had to do was make a run behind Morgan Rogers, whose defensive awareness was on show with England in the last international break but less so here for Chelsea. King blasted on an angle and from 16 yards, and Robert Sanchez was beaten at his near post as Alonso clocked why this goalkeeper is not for him.

2 – Fulham, Gonzalo Garcia, 54th minute, for 3-2 to Chelsea

While Chelsea binned Sanchez and replaced him with Emiliano Martinez after this game, this goal involved an error from a centre-back, first and foremost. Colwill failed to deal with a long ball, heading fresh air rather than clearing, then Sanchez spilled his save for Garcia’s rebound.

3 – Brighton, Malick Yalcouye, 35th minute, for 3-1 to Chelsea

This originated from a long throw taken quickly in Brighton’s own half and sent down the line. Pedro Neto flew across to try to tackle on the wing, but forgot to take the actual ball. Yalcouye charged forward and played in Charalampos Kostoulas, who ran behind Maxence Lacroix. His shot was saved, but Yalcouye finished with oomph as the ball pinged in off the post.

4 – Brighton, Joao Pedro own goal, 63rd minute, for 3-2 to Chelsea

An unfortunate deflection from Joao Pedro as Pascal Gross took aim. In the build-up, Cole Palmer neglected his defensive duties by allowing Gross to run behind him, much like Rogers v Fulham the week before. The nick from Joao Pedro wrongfooted Martinez in goal. It happens.

Chelsea's vulnerabilities were on show as they overcame Brighton 4-3 back in August

5 – Brighton, Pascal Gross, 96th minute, for 4-3 to Chelsea

A long throw. A spot of head tennis with Valentin Barco initially beaten in the air by Diego Gomez. Then Gross nods beyond Martinez as Joao Pedro asks Rogers why he didn’t have him. A soft consolation to concede.

6 – Arsenal, Kai Havertz, 25th minute, for 1-1

This one was largely on the goalkeeping as a few wondered whether Martinez was Sanchez in disguise. Havertz dashed inside from the right wing and away from Fofana, then scored from 18 yards into the small sliver of light available at Martinez’s near post. With that, Chelsea's lead was lost.

7 – Arsenal, Martin Odegaard, 50th minute, for 2-1 to Arsenal

Sometimes, you just have to say the opposition's move worked well, and this was a fine one from Arsenal rather than a defensive disasterclass per se, even if Fofana was fooled by Havertz’s dummy. That allowed the pass from Christos Tzolis to roll through to Odegaard to score the winner after Reece James had not spied how his fellow captain was unmarked in front of him.

8 – Hull, Mohamed Belloumi, 28th minute, for 1-1

Do not let the ball bounce. That is defending 101. The no-no we are all taught as kids. Jorrel Hato broke that basic rule here. Hato let the ball bounce in front of him and loop over him after it was launched into the box from the left wing by Ryan Giles, with Chelsea’s other full back Malo Gusto having failed to stop that cross from coming. Belloumi was waiting behind Hato to score. Hato was hooked at half-time for good reason.

Mohamed Belloumi scored the first of two goals for Hull against the Blues after Jorrel Hato allowed the ball to bounce in the box

9 – Hull, Mohamed Belloumi, 34th minute, for 2-1 to Hull

Martinez came to clear Hull's corner. He didn’t. He flapped as Semi Ajayi, who did not even have a marker on him as Colwill and Fofana were marking zonally rather than taking care of the 6ft 4in centre-back, headed into the crossbar. The rebound fell to Belloumi, who, unmarked at the edge of the box, scored via two deflections which made Chelsea’s six-yard box resemble a pinball machine. Not a good look for Austin MacPhee, the new set-piece specialist.

10 – Brentford, Jaidon Anthony, 61st minute, for 1-0 to Brentford

Another one which MacPhee will want to leave off the showreel. The corner came in. It went to the back of the pack. It was headed back across by Jannik Schuster, then in by Anthony. Fofana, Lacroix and Danny Welbeck formed a nice little triangle around the attacker without anyone ever actually marking him.

11 – Brentford, Igor Thiago, 83rd minute, for 2-0 to Brentford

Jordan Henderson tried and failed to punch a pass forward. It turned over possession, and Brentford countered. Chelsea had a high line as they were pushing for the equaliser, which was understandable. One lovely through-ball from Mikkel Damsgaard later, Kevin Schade was through. Martinez denied him one-v-one, but Thiago finished the rebound.

12 – Brentford, Fabio Carvalho, 94th minute, for 3-0 to Brentford

It originated from a long throw, cleared partially by Chelsea but recycled to the wing by Brentford. A low cross came in with a deflection from Josh Acheampong helping it find Carvalho, who had sneaked in behind Pep Chavarria.

Fabio Carvalho scored Brentford's final goal in their 3-0 win in September after sneaking in at the back post, after Chelsea only partially cleared from a long throw

13 – Bournemouth, Evanilson, 51st minute, for 3-1 to Chelsea

Never let it be said that Chelsea do not give confidence to strikers. Evanilson had not scored in the Premier League since February 2026. Then he visited Stamford Bridge in this fixture in October. Since then, he has scored in every league game played, now on six in a row. This goal came from a Bournemouth corner. It was flicked on at the front of the pack. Moises Caicedo tried to clear the ball amid a goalmouth melee, but only blasted his clearance into Evanilson for a gimme of a goal.

14 – Tottenham, Mike Penders own goal, 77th minute, for 1-0 to Tottenham

Whatever you do, when starting in the Premier League for the first time and against your side’s fiercest rivals no less, do not punch the ball into your own goal. Anyway, Penders came for a corner, and you know what happened next. It did not help that the 21-year-old goalkeeper was challenged by Jan Paul van Hecke, who was allowed a free run at him after being left by Lacroix, but even so. This was a horrific moment for Penders, and happened despite Chelsea trying that trick where they send players out of the box to ease the congestion.

15 – Tottenham, Mathys Tel, 87th minute, for 2-0 to Tottenham

Acheampong lost the ball over on the right wing and couldn’t catch up with Tel as he flew forward. There was a weak attempt at a tackle by Lacroix, who almost sheepishly stuck out a lazy leg. Then Tel scored from 25 yards as Alonso violated a non-negotiable: you do not lose at home to Tottenham.

Mike Penders punched a corner into his own net as Chelsea suffered a rare home loss to Tottenham

16 – Sunderland, Enzo Le Fee, 36th minute, for 1-0 to Sunderland

A penalty, but we will analyse the build-up. Colwill in particular had been getting bullied by Brobbey in this game. So much so that he went on to be hooked at half-time while on a yellow. On this occasion, Sunderland launched a long ball towards Brobbey, who used his strength to turn Colwill and charge into the box. He then dropped down – controversially so as Chelsea did not believe it warranted a spot-kick. Le Fee stepped up, and scored the game’s only goal.

17 – Leeds, Noah Okafor, 28th minute, for 1-1

Chelsea fans could take their pick of players to blame here. First, there was Fofana not heading back James Trafford’s long ball from whence it came. One of Willie Isa’s jobs as Chelsea’s ‘cultural architect’ is to act as a human shield while the defenders practise winning headers in their warm-up. They still seem to mess up a fair few mid-match, as Fofana did here. Then there was Acheampong letting the ball bounce over him à la Hato, and Colwill backtracking as if stuck in reverse. All three were surrounding Okafor as he then made it 1-1. Martinez did not even attempt to dive as the ball rolled by him. Colwill appeared to ask him why as Leeds celebrated. Excruciating by everyone involved.

18 – Leeds, Dominic Calvert-Lewin, 53rd minute, for 2-1 to Leeds

Another penalty, but one which we believe should not have been awarded for a handball by Rogers. It was given by Michael Oliver in real time, and backed up by Michael Salisbury on VAR. Any reasonable fan would hate it if this was given against their club. Anyway, it all originated from a long throw. Three Chelsea players tried to head it clear at the same time – good communication, lads – and they failed as Fofana only flicked it on behind him. What followed was this gift of a spot-kick, which Calvert-Lewin scored for 2-1.

19 – Leeds, Noah Okafor, 58th minute, for 3-1 to Leeds

Yet more ball-watching from Chelsea’s defenders as opposed to taking note of the chap that had already scored one goal lining up for his second. Okafor was always unmarked as he moved into the box from around the penalty spot to meet Ethan Ampadu’s deflected cross.

20 – Leeds, Brenden Aaronson, 91st minute, for 4-1 to Leeds

A ball forward from Leeds left Colwill in a bind. Because he was supposed to have both Calvert-Lewin and Harry Wilson, he was stuck in between, and actually had neither. Calvert-Lewin headed to Wilson, who had time to pick his pass. Gusto, on as a substitute, noticed Aaronson making a burst in behind Chelsea’s back line. He tried to play him offside by suddenly stopping running with him but timed it wrong. Aaronson was onside. Gusto raced to try to stop him, but the Leeds attacker simply checked back inside, and scored through the legs of Martinez, who gave the woodwork a kicking in frustration.

#949. China’s AI-powered smart-city model is going global

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jacob Dreyer is an editor for business, economics, politics and law at Palgrave (a subsidiary of Springer Nature) based in Shanghai, China. The views expressed here are his own.

To understand the Chinese smart city, it helps to know that twenty-first-century infrastructure, technology and policy increasingly makes the whole of China a single, interconnected economic unit. Trains, planes and autonomous vehicles shuttle about, with the centre of megacities such as Shanghai and Shenzhen merely being in the middle of ‘one-hour circles’ for commuters that allow them to reach anywhere in the wider urban area with ease. Previous barriers to the internal movement of workers, such the hukou system, which restricted access to public services based on a person’s birthplace, are being removed, making it easier for people to compete for jobs across the country. And all the while, the Internet supercharges these shifts to a nationwide marketplace, backed by an ever-expanding supply of data centres. Sichuanese farmers of organic lemons now livestream from rural villages on apps such as Xiaohongshu or Douyin as they compete for city restaurateurs to buy their products.

So, if the goal of a ‘smart city’ is to use big data and AI to outsource governance functions, keeping everything running smoothly, then maybe we should think of China as a single city, with its different provinces and megalopolises as neighbourhoods with their own special roles. For instance, three of China’s megacities each have their own important function: Beijing regulates and invests in fundamental research; Shanghai is home to multinational corporations, frontier research in AI and biotech, and finance; and the Greater Bay Area, including Shenzhen and Guangzhou, is home to innovative manufacturers, such as electric vehicle producer BYD, tech giant Huawei and consumer electronics firm DJI.

China’s 15th five-year plan unveiled earlier this year sees the country in this way, too, by entrusting certain functions to different cities and regions, and with rural areas also playing an essential role. In the northeast, farming is increasingly carried out with the use of drones and big data by state-owned companies such as Beidahuang. In Inner Mongolia and Xinjiang, data centres are powered by abundant solar and wind energy, where they calculate how the self-driving cars of China’s eastern seaboard should navigate roads or process the AI that helps to keep the country’s state-of-the-art high-speed train network running on time.

This approach on data is embodied by 东数西算 (roughly translated as ‘east data, west compute’), a national-level strategic project to channel data from developed eastern regions to resource-rich western regions for processing and storage using eight data-centre ‘hubs’ located across the country. Eastern megacities generate the vast majority of China’s data and AI requests, but they bring skyrocketing land costs, power shortages and cooling difficulties that make hosting data centres unattractive. Instead, the solar farms of Xinjiang’s deserts and the wind farms of the Mongolian steppe are used to provide renewable, cheap energy to data centres.

One key example is Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia, which has been transformed from a traditional farming region into a prominent data powerhouse, earning the name ‘Grassland Cloud Valley’. The energy costs in Ulanqab are low, because the government has been installing massive renewable capacity, relying on the area’s abundant wind and solar resources. Mongolia is cold for most of the year, so data centres use standard air cooling rather than massive air-conditioning set-ups — effectively, they just cover the servers with plastic and leave the door open for wintry winds to circulate. Major firms such as Huawei, Alibaba, Kuaishou and Apple have constructed large-scale cloud bases in Ulanqab. The region houses China’s largest intelligent computing centre for autonomous driving (Fuyao), built by Xpeng Motors and Alibaba Cloud, which has helped make it 170 times faster to train self-driving models. It means an autonomous taxi driving around Beijing is effectively being controlled by servers in the far-away desert of Inner Mongolia.

#948. Why Man City can't wear their new kit in Premier League

Manchester City will only be wearing their orange kit for selected Champions League games

Manchester City sported a new orange fourth kit during their Champions League draw with Napoli on Tuesday - but will not be able to wear it in the Premier League.

Top-flight clubs in England can only wear a maximum of three strips in a league campaign, meaning Enzo Maresca's side cannot play in their new kit.

However, there is no limit in the Champions League, meaning City can wear their new strip for the rest of their European campaign.

City can also wear the kit in the FA Cup, provided that an application is made to the Football Association, as well as a reason for its requested use.

That is why Arsenal were allowed to play in a white fourth strip in the 2025-26 FA Cup as part of their campaign to combat youth knife crime in London.

Fans could scan the badge on City's 2025-26 fourth kit to receive items in a video game

City also released a green fourth kit in 2025-26 with a gaming-inspired theme.

The kit, debuted during their Champions League victory over Villarreal, featured an NFC chip in the club badge that fans could scan to unlock gaming rewards.

The club released another fourth kit in the 2024-25 season co-designed by Noel Gallagher in tribute to the 30th anniversary of Oasis' 1994 album 'Definitely Maybe'.

It was worn in the Champions League by the men's team against Inter Milan and Paris St-Germain, and the women's team against Paris FC and Barcelona.

A fifth kit was also used by the men's team during the 2025 Club World Cup

During the 2023-24 season, the women's side also sported a Chinese New Year-inspired shirt in a League Cup victory against rivals Manchester United.

While the Premier League is more restrictive over the number of kits that can be released - the rules are more relaxed in other European leagues.

Napoli wore 13 strips during the 2021-22 season; including a Halloween kit, four different Diego Maradona tributes and four Europa League-specific kits.

#947. Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

Felix Nmecha's "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

#946. Thomas Frank earns his first Crystal Palace victory as boss, Bournemouth win TENTH game in a row with comeback, and Brighton thrash Romanian minnows - but Sunderland are held at home

By LUKE POWER, SPORTS REPORTER and BEN WINSTANLEY and WILL PICKWORTH, SPORTS REPORTER and MILES STARFORTH

Published: 15:09 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 19:33 EST, 26 November 2026

Thomas Frank said he was happy to be 'back in the circus' at his Crystal Palace unveiling, yet when he found himself staring down the barrel at a second defeat in a week, he may have been rueing that statement.

But when Chris Richards' long-throw made its way to Jean-Philippe Mateta, everything changed on a chaotic night at Selhurst Park.

The French forward was pulled down by Jon Martin, who was sent off, and after Mateta tucked away his penalty, a flat performance and atmosphere was transformed.

Having been dominated, Palace were now quick, confident and incisive, and it was the Basque outfit who were on the ropes as Daichi Kamada saw an effort cleared off the line.

Jorgen Strand Larsen then attempted an audacious bicycle kick which fell to the feet of Dwight McNeil yards out to send the home fans into delirium.

It could have been more, but Yeremy Pino's penalty in added time was saved and Strand Larsen missed an open goal. Dean Henderson then made a brilliant stop to secure the three points.

Thomas Frank got his first win as Crystal Palace boss as his side came from behind to beat Real Sociedad 2-1

Palace's season has been a disaster thus far, but it now has lift-off, and most importantly belief, heading into Sunday's crunch clash with Hull.

'It could be (a turning point) but we need to follow it up with a good performance against Hull,' said Frank. 'But you can take a lot of positives. What I really liked is the belief from the players and that we were a threat on set pieces.

'The penalty and red card changed the game. It’s not easy 10 vs 11, but we were brave and it paid off - and then we were all close to a heart attack in the last five minutes!'

Frank, who received a warm reception from the Eagles faithful ahead of his first home game, handed rare starts to Will Hughes, Ben Chilwell and Eddie Nketiah as he rang the changes after last week’s defeat by Coventry.

They practised defending set-pieces in the warm-up in an attempt to deal with what has become their kryptonite, yet Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr almost turned in at the far post from a free kick just minutes in.

After a poor opening half hour, Sociedad stepped things up and Henderson was forced into a string of good saves. Palace’s midfield was struggling and the Basque outfit should have gone ahead when Mikel Oyarzabal somehow fired straight at Henderson from a few yards out.

The England keeper had to be alert again soon after, yet the pressure paid off when Sarr turned home from Job Ochieng's cross.

But the game changed with Mateta's intervention, before McNeil ensured that, despite the injury-time mayhem, Frank is more than happy to be back in the madhouse of management.

'The feeling after a win on the pitch with players, staff and fans, but also in the changing room is so difficult to describe - it’s so unique,' said Frank. 'You like to experience a lot of that, but the hectic last 15 minutes, that was crazy.'

'The red card and penalty were the decisive action in the match,' added Sociedad boss Pellegrino Matarazzo. 'We controlled the match completely up until that. We tried to stabilise, but we could not hold them off long enough.'

Can anybody stop Bournemouth? For long stretches here it looked as if their relentless march would finally be stopped - but the 10-man Cherries found another gear to continue their rampage.

Marco Rose’s men have won 10 games in a row now, extending a club record. For two months, they have steamrolled their opponents with dauntless football and racked up an aggregate score of 25-3. They sit top of the Europa League with a perfect record.

Underneath the red and black armour, fans are starting to wonder if these players are actually of our species. Is Justin Kluivert a man or a cyborg? If you prick James Hill, does he bleed?

With each victory, the cry of the football world grows louder: somebody, please, stop this Bournemouth juggernaut, for the sake of everybody else’s trophy prospects.

Celta Vigo stepped up as the next challengers and thought they would be the heroes. They found Bournemouth’s net four times in all, but were denied by the offside flag for three of them. For long stretches, they were in command.

Bournemouth have now won 10 games in a row after coming from behind to beat Celta Vigo 2-1

After a disappointing first half, Alvaro Rodriguez got them level early in the second

Rayan scored the winner against the run of play as Bournemouth continued their perfect run in the Europa League

In the first half, Bournemouth looked average. They were gifting away the ball in their own half, Celta found ways to sneak through their pincer-movement press, and the Spaniards had the better chances.

The first red flag came 11 minutes in, when Michele Di Gregorio spilled a save into the path of Pablo Duran, who dinked over the goalkeeper but saw his effort ruled out for offside.

Such warning bells were unheeded. Not long later, former Liverpool man Iago Aspas forced a save with a spectacular overhead kick at the age of 39.

Bournemouth failed to clear their lines, and Aspas punished the visitors, ghosting past Alex Scott on his return from injury before blasting beyond Di Gregorio with his left foot.

Things went from bad to worse minutes later when Bafode Diakite was sent off for a stamp on Couhaib Driouech, his yellow card upgraded to a red after a review by referee Harm Osmers.

Celta almost doubled their lead when Duran beat Di Gregorio again, but he had strayed offside.

The cameras panned to Rose, who stood looking bewildered on the sidelines, hands on hips. It took them 37 minutes for Kluivert to register their first shot. Bournemouth had been played off the park. This was a case of clinging on.

But the side that emerged in the second half were unrecognisable. If Bournemouth were a man down, they played with all the swagger of having an extra body.

They were level within two minutes of the restart, Alvaro Rodriguez glancing in from Amine Adli’s header.

Suddenly Bournemouth were their efflorescent selves again. Antonio Silva, Adli, and Rodriguez combined for a beautiful passage of play but were spurned by the offside flag. Hill tested Ionut Radu from range.

They finally got their rewards on the counter-attack, when Marcus Tavernier teed up his fellow substitute Rayan to slot past Radu and stun their hosts. Another comeback job complete.

And so the Bournemouth army marches on unfettered. In the next nine days, they face Fulham, Brighton, and Hull in the Premier League. By the time they visit Arsenal in mid-December, they may be breathing down their necks.

Earlier this week, Brighton CEO Paul Barber revealed the lengths that his club go to before agreeing to sign a player.

'We try and talk to people that know them, people that have coached them, people that played with them, sponsors that have worked with them, media that have interviewed them, maybe even neighbours that have lived next door to them,' he told Men in Blazers media network. 'You know, what sort of people are we talking about? Are we talking about players that are entirely focused on their work?'

There can be little doubt that the rigorous selection process is working, and two of their budget buys were on the scoresheet in the first half as they made light work of the Romanian champions Universitatea Craiova - and continued to make a mockery of the supposed challenge of balancing domestic and European assaults.

In the third minute Ibrahim Osman - £16.6m from Nordsjaelland in 2024 – finished off a sharp team move from close range after a pinpoint Jack Hinshelwood cross. Then shortly after the half-hour mark full back Maxime de Cuyper, £17m from Club Brugge in 2025, seized on a slack defensive ball into midfield, took two touches in advancing forward and - still well outside the box – wrongfooted the goalkeeper as he stroked the ball into the far corner. He made the finish look much easier than it was.

Brighton thrashed Romanian champions Universitatea Craiova and look capable of competing on multiple fronts

If the result was still in any doubt then, it wasn’t by the 39th minute when Vladimir Screciu was sent off for a clumsy challenge on Matt O’Riley. Referee Matthias Jollenbeck showed a yellow card but a replay showed a hefty tread on the ankle and - after being sent to his monitor - upgraded it to red.

The second half, then, gave the Seagulls a chance to remind everyone of their ruthless side. Already the highest scorers in the Premier League - averaging 2.4 per game this season – they wasted little time adding to their tally.

First, 19-year-old Charalampos Kostoulas made it three with his sixth of the season thanks to a cool finish on the hour mark, two minutes before Osman – like Hinshelwood a constant menace - picked the ball up on the left and cut inside to roll home his second.

They ended 90 minutes of domination having had 27 shots – one of which saw Femi Azeez missing the chance to make it five on debut by inexplicably blazing over from five yards.

Brighton have now scored four or more in five of their eight home games this season, and ended last night’s rout top of the Conference League having yet to concede a goal. The competition does not look big enough for them.

Sunderland still have work to do if the club is to reach the Europa League’s knockout stages after Jagiellonia Bialystok held them to a 1-1 draw in a game which saw some supporters of the Polish club evade a UEFA ban and get into the Stadium of Light.

Timur Tutierov’s second-half opener for Sunderland, hoping to secure a top-eight finish in the competition’s league phase and avoid the play-offs in their first European campaign in 53 years, was quickly cancelled out by the visitors.

‘It’s clear we are making many unforced errors this season leading to goals,’ said head coach Regis Le Bris. ‘The last two games, it didn’t happen, which is good, and now this is a reminder you can’t relax.’

Jagiellonia supporters had been banned from the game following crowd disturbances at the club’s fixture away to Levski Sofia on November 5.

But a number of visiting fans were removed from the stadium by police during the first half, and a “disappointed” Sunderland issued a statement after the game which claimed that Jagiellonia had “failed to engage and cooperate” with efforts to stop their supporters getting into home sections.

Le Bris had gone into the game without injured captain Granit Xhaka and striker Brian Brobbey, two of his most influential players. Sunderland’s head coach, mindful of forthcoming Premier League games against Tottenham Hotspur, Liverpool and Newcastle United, took no chances with the pair for the visit of Jagiellonia, ninth in the Polish league.

Sunderland had to settle for a 1-1 draw against Polish side Jagiellonia Bialystok

He made six changes from the team which had held Aston Villa to a goalless draw at the weekend, again fielding a youthful team in the competition.

A flat performance from a much-changed team had seen Sunderland beaten 2-0 by Croatian champions Dinamo Zagreb in their last European outing at the Stadium of Light. The visiting section had been bouncing that night, in contrast to the empty seats for the visit of Jagiellonia.

On Wearside, the feeling ahead of the match was that third-bottom Sunderland, while shot shy, were slowly turning a corner, having taken four points from fixtures against Chelsea and Villa without conceding a goal to climb above Manchester United in the table.

The big one in Europe - AC Milan at the San Siro - is next in the competition for Sunderland, with the fixture having captured the imagination of supporters.

There were scarves with the slogan ‘Have you ever seen a Mackem in Milan? You’re about to!’ on sale outside the ground, with the merchandise a nod to a song which fans of their rivals Newcastle United can no longer sing.

Sunderland had an early scare when a Nik Prelec shot took a deflection off Ndah Sidiki, but Robin Roefs was able to gather the ball.

Within minutes of the game starting, it became apparent that a group of Polish fans had managed to buy tickets in the North Stand, and police were quickly called to remove them from the stadium amid cheers from Sunderland supporters.

On the pitch, it was another slow start for Le Bris’ side, though Malick Fofana tested Slawomir Abramowicz with a fine left-footed shot from outside the box.

Timur Tutierov was on target fo the Black Cats, but this was a flat performance

Enzo Le Fee did well to seize on a back pass in the 30th minute and cross from the left for Nilson Angulo - who was unmarked in the box - after rounding the goalkeeper. However, his shot struck the feet of Yuki Kobayashi.

Omar Alderete was forced off as the half-time break approached, and Roefs beat away a free-kick from Kajetan Szmyt.

Sunderland went into the break knowing they should have led, but their finishing had again let them down in the absence of Brobbey, their talisman.

Le Bris’ team were ahead within seconds of the restart. Rigg broke through the middle, and the ball was worked to Le Fee, whose cross bounced off a visiting defender on its way to Tutierov at the far post, who headed home.

The lead did not last, with Kamil Jozwiak seizing on a Nilson Reinildo backpass before rounding Roefs to level.

Roefs denied Jozwiak at the hour-mark with a low save as home fans became increasingly frustrated with their team.

A frustrated Le Bris said: ‘It’s hard to take, because we would like to have better football, better expression.’
