#911. Can Beijing scale up its smart-city ambitions?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hepeng Jia is a freelance science writer based in Suzhou, China.

Yizhuang, the district of Beijing where this Lingyi iTech robotics factory is located, is a key area of the city for demonstrating leading smart-city solutions.Credit: Qilai Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images

In Yizhuang, a high-tech industrial zone in Beijing, drivers have access to parts of roads, highways and intersections where they might experience green lights all the way. Networks of road cameras and sensors feed data to a local control centre, which issues app notifications to drivers about upcoming interruptions, recommended driving speeds and lane suggestions to keep the traffic moving. On these ‘green-wave corridors’, the average number of traffic stops throughout the day has dropped by 40.6%, and the average travel speed has increased by 15.1%, according to local reports.

Also known as the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, or Beijing E-Town, Yizhuang was created in the early 1990s by the Beijing Municipal People’s Government to act as the city’s leading smart-city demonstration zone. Alongside its intelligent transport systems, it has become a key area for autonomous-vehicle development and robotics, often showcasing emerging technologies at public events.

The annual Beijing E-Town Half-Marathon, for example, attracts hundreds of humanoid robots built by companies and university teams to compete with humans over an almost 22-kilometre track. In 2025, the inaugural year of the race, many robots failed to finish. But in this year’s race, held in April, the robots showed major improvements in speed, reliability and autonomy.

Alongside Yizhuang, Beijing has many other smart-city ‘brains’ — hubs of innovation that are fast-tracking technological development in strategic areas such as artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure and data governance.

One such area is Haidian in northwest Beijing, which runs a spatial-mapping platform that functions as a digital twin of the district. Gathering data from some 170,000 buildings, plus tens of thousands of road cameras and sensors, the platform flags local faults and automatically generates work orders to speed up repairs. The repair-response time for missing manhole covers, for instance, which is a major hazard for drivers and pedestrians, has been reduced from a whole day to just four hours. Haidian is home to Peking University and Tsinghua University — two of China’s leading academic institutions in the Nature Index — as well as the country’s greatest concentration of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) institutes.

Underpinning Beijing’s smart-city ambitions is its enormous investment in science and technology. Beijing has been the leading science city in the Nature Index since 2016, and in 2025, its Share in the natural and health sciences was about two-thirds higher than that of its closest competitor, Shanghai. That year, Beijing spent around 6% of its gross domestic product on R&D — the highest share in the country. The city’s sprawling research system has formed close ties with its private AI sector, which, as of 2024, encompassed about 2,400 companies worth nearly 350 billion yuan (US$51.7 billion).

A key challenge for Beijing is how to link all of the data being collected by its various districts and zones. Different departments might not feel incentivized to share their data or link up with central databases, says Yuan Zhibin, a senior research fellow at the CAS Institute of Science and Technology Strategy Consulting in Beijing. Strong competition between Beijing’s leading technology districts, such as Yizhuang and Haidian, as well as the costs involved in changing or updating systems, are major factors, says Yuan.

#908. Referee being 'drunk' claims are 'entirely unfounded'

Hanna Hattab has refereed in a number of competitions run by the Asian Football Confederation

Claims that a referee was drunk during an Asian Football Confederation (AFC) Champions League Two match are "entirely unfounded", officials say.

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab was replaced at half-time of the match between Iran's Gol Gohar and Al Jazira of the United Arab Emirates.

Reports claimed Gol Gohar staff accused the referee of being drunk following what has been described as some erratic decision-making in the first half.

Iranian news agency ISNA quoted one club official as saying: "The referee was not in a normal state," and suggesting they would not have played on had the referee not been removed.

Accusations of drunkenness were also widely shared on social media.

But Hattab, who is part of the AFC's elite refereeing group, has released a statement denying the allegation, saying he has been defamed and threatening legal action.

The fourth official took over for the second half, with Al Jazira winning the match.

Hattab said he will be "issuing an official statement that clarifies all the details and facts related to what happened".

Omani sports journalist Issa Said, who covers Asian competitions, claimed on social media that what happened to Hattab was "due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus".

"He underwent a medical examination after the match and was not intoxicated, contrary to what has been circulating."

In their statement on the match, which was played in Asia's second tier continental competition, the Syrian Football Association backed Hattab.

"Following an assessment of his health, it has been confirmed - contrary to various claims circulating on social media - that the reports regarding his situation are entirely unfounded," they wrote.

"The Committee reiterates its unwavering support for him and is committed to thoroughly investigating all details and circumstances surrounding the incident."

#907. Why Cambridgeshire derby could be season-defining

Robbie Savage's Peterborough United will seek to defend a long unbeaten home record in the Cambridgeshire derby when Neil Harris's U's visit London Road

Local derbies are always special, but none more so than when they have the ability to shape the narrative of a season. This much is true of Saturday's Cambridgeshire derby (12:30 GMT).

Robbie Savage's Peterborough United welcome Neil Harris' Cambridge United to London Road with both at something of a crossroads.

At stake for Posh? Their League One status. Despite an impressive win at Plymouth Argyle last time out, they remain 22nd in the table and need results to avoid a battle against the drop being the defining theme of their season.

As for the U's, the derby presents an opportunity to regain momentum. After October's 2-1 win at Barnsley they were one point off top spot, but failure to pick up three points in any of their five league games since leaves them caught between play-off contention and mid-table drift.

The derby also carries the weight of recent history, with the emotional baggage greater for the U's.

They have lost each of their past seven away league games against Peterborough, losing those matches by a combined 20-3 scoreline.

Indeed, they have not won at London Road since an FA Cup tie in 1994-95, while their wait for a league win at their rivals' home extends to 1990.

Savage, appointed last month, said his side were well aware of their responsibility for continuing that record.

"We don't want to be the group that loses to Cambridge at home, first time in 30 years I think it would be," he said.

"We don't want to be that group. We want to put three, four, five past them and win the game. Even if it's 1-0, it doesn't matter.

"It's all about winning, don't care we win, just win the game."

Robbie Savage: 'We want to turn the county blue'

The victory at Plymouth ended a four-game wait for a win, and Savage said the onus was on his side to back it up on derby day. If they do, they know they will have secured successive league victories for the first time since February.

"This game is at the top of the mountain," he said.

"No doubt about it. The players will be up for it, we've shown them videos of the previous games, we've got fans sending messages.

"We're doing everything we can to make them realise how big this game is. It's not another game, it's the derby. A great game.

"Neil knows what it means. We're two passionate managers. He's done far better than me as a manager so far, so hats off to him. But we both want to win.

"They will bring 1,600 fans and we need to show Cambridge that we want to county to be blue."

Neil Harris: 'We'll attack the game like no other'

While this derby is new territory for Savage, Harris comes armed with the memory of defeat in his only previous taste of the tie in a season than ultimately ended with relegation for the U's.

After securing a return to the third-tier in 2025-26 - and having made a competitive start to this campaign - there is no shortage of motivation to deliver a long-awaited win for his side.

"It is a one-off fixture," he told BBC Look East.

"There is a slightly different feel and mentality to it, but it means a hell of a lot to a hell of a lot of people.

"It means a lot to get bragging rights over a direct opponent. It's important to get back to our highest standards."

Posh have lost just one of their past 12 league games against Cambridge United, winning their past four in succession.

But with Savage's side in a precarious league position, there is optimism among fans that their 36-year long wait to celebrate a league win at London Road could finally arrive.

"It's about playing with heart and emotion, but brains as well," added Harris.

"We understand the importance of the fixture, I understand it as a driven manager. It's about trying to make sure we make our fans proud."

#906. Hearts' European hopes hang by a thread but Vrancken proud

Hearts' hopes of a memorable draw with Monaco were dashed in the 94th minute

There was a bittersweet feeling at Tynecastle after Folarin Balogun's 94th-minute winner preserved Monaco's perfect Conference League record and condemned Hearts to a third defeat from four.

Wouter Vrancken's side had gone toe-to-toe with one of the best teams in the tournament, scored two glorious goals, but ultimately came away with nothing for their efforts.

Now they have little to no margin for error in their two remaining league phase matches.

They will likely have to beat both Borac Banja Luka of Bosnia and Cyprus' Pafos to reach the knockout stages, but if they perform as they did against Monaco, they will give themselves a fighting chance.

Hearts have garnered a reputation as entertainers under Vrancken - scoring a raft of goals while being porous at the back.

This game was their season in microcosm. The goals - scored by Jordi Altena and Sabah Kerjota - were things of beauty, picture-perfect strikes worthy of any stage.

But as thrilling as Hearts were in attack, they were as baffling at the back.

Jamie McCart unnecessarily tripped Matthis Abline, allowing Balogun to score from the penalty spot and Monaco's second came from Altena giving the ball away.

"It's Gladiators - are we not entertained? It's sensational," said Hearts legend John Robertson at half-time, with the game finely poised at 2-2.

Monaco strike in 94th minute to break Hearts in five-goal epic

Latest Hearts news, analysis and fan views

Both teams had chances to win it in the second half, but it was Monaco who took theirs in the final stages. Mamadou Coulibaly was afforded too much space and he slipped Balogun through to beat Beau Reus.

"It's a lack of nous and a little bit of naivety," former Hearts midfielder Michael Stewart said on TNT Sports. "McCart backs off and allows the ball to be played into Balogun's feet."

Despite the frustrating nature of the late concession, Vrancken's overwhelming emotion was of pride.

"I'm very disappointed with how we give the goal away at the end," he said.

"The biggest thing is the pride for the performance today. Against a side of Monaco's [quality] - we're still missing nine players through injury - this performance was really pleasing."

Before the recent international break, Hearts were beaten 3-1 by Swiss outfit Thun, before a shock 5-2 home defeat by high-flying Falkirk in the Scottish Premiership.

However, they bounced back with a ruthless 8-0 win at Dundee on Saturday and carried that confidence into this game against a team with a far bigger budget.

"You saw that the confidence was there from the weekend and there was conviction around their box," Vrancken added. "It will not work every time, but the conviction and energy was there again.

"Our team kept their heads in the game and kept going for it, not being pleased with 2-2. Really pleased with what I saw."

Aside from his dismay at Balogun's winner and how it came about, Vrancken's main gripe was with the officials.

He felt there was a foul on Kerjota in the build-up to Monaco's second goal and was bemused at the fact neither Takumi Minamino and Denis Zakaria were sent off.

Minamino - already on a yellow card - wiped out Sabri Guendouz on the edge of the Monaco box, but got away with a warning. And VAR opted not to intervene after Zakaria went over the top of the ball and caught Pierre Landry Kabore on the shin.

"The second goal, they pulled Sabah [Kerjota] and he can't do his defensive work," Vrancken said.

"It was not the only refereeing decision that was interesting tonight. I don't know how it's possible not to give a red card for the tackle on [Pierre Landry Kabore]. It's clearly above the ankle, so it's always a red card.

"And why didn't Minamino get a second yellow before half-time? He prevents a shot from Sabri at the edge of the box.

"The explanation of the fourth official was even more crazy - he explained it could be for his first yellow card, but not for his second yellow. It was clearly a yellow card and then we were against 10 in the second half."

#905. What are fossil fuels?

They are in our shampoo bottles, power our cars and heat our homes. But what actually are fossil fuels, and why do they matter?

Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

They started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

Fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete plan, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national plans.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said.

#904. Lammens - the Man Utd goalkeeper under scrutiny like never before

Senne Lammens (left) joined Manchester United in the summer of 2025

After a first season at Manchester United that drew little but praise, goalkeeper Senne Lammens is under the microscope like never before.

A bad mistake that gifted Sporting their second goal on Wednesday, having earlier conceded a clumsy penalty, followed several other errors so far this season.

The 24-year-old Belgium international also made an error at the World Cup in the summer, spilling a shot that led to Spain's winning goal in the 88th minute of their quarter-final.

"I don't know [at what point Manchester United drop him]," legendary Manchester United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel told CBS Sports on Wednesday.

"Mauricio Pochettino has come in and brought his own staff. That means he's got a new goalkeeping coach and maybe that is something that can change it for him.

"[At the World Cup] he came on against Spain and made a bit of a mistake. Mikel Merino scored and they got knocked out. I feel he's lost a little bit of confidence from that mistake and hasn't really recovered.

"As a goalkeeper, when you're not on your best form, you need your defenders in front of you to help you out. The sad truth is that they haven't been able to do that and that makes it so much worse. I like him a lot but today was not a great day for him."

Director of football Jason Wilcox and United's data team overruled Ruben Amorim when they opted to sign Lammens from Royal Antwerp for Â£18.1m in September 2025.

Amorim wanted Argentina World Cup winner Emiliano Martinez, who was left waiting for a deadline day call that never came to seal a move from Aston Villa.

United felt Lammens had the attributes to become one of the world's best goalkeepers. At 24, he is still young. Schmeichel was 27 when he joined United in 1991. Edwin van der Sar was 34 when he left Fulham in 2005. Both had hundreds of senior appearances behind them. Lammens has just over 100, more than half of them with Royal Antwerp.

Although he made the odd error last season, Lammens did nothing to suggest Wilcox and co had got it wrong.

After releasing Turkey international Altay Bayindir, who replaced Andre Onana as first choice at the start of last season and is back on loan in Turkey with Trabzonspor, they signed 36-year-old Wales international Karl Darlow as back-up this term.

Darlow finished last season as first choice at Leeds. But he only started 30 league games in three seasons with the Elland Road outfit. Also on the bench in Lisbon was Tom Heaton. The 40-year-old has not played in a senior game since February 2023.

Mistakes earlier in the season â former United midfielder Paul Scholes claimed in September '"the jury is still out" on whether Lammens is truly top class â have brought increased analysis. His positioning for Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal for Liverpool on Sunday was questioned externally, even if United focused their attentions on Bradley Barcola shoving into the wall.

Just 75 seconds after getting down to make an excellent save from Luis Suarez's first penalty, Lammens recklessly charged out and upended Maxi Araujo, even though Noussair Mazraoui seemed to be in a position to deal with it.

Then, after two Bruno Fernandes goals at the start of the second period had turned the Champions League tie in the visitors' favour, Lammens reached to collect a high ball and inexplicably dropped it in front of Suarez, who applied the overhead kick finish.

Understandably, there was sympathy in the dressing room.

"This team is a family," said striker Joshua Zirkzee. "There's no-one who will suffer by themselves.

"Senne is a great goalkeeper and mistakes happen. In this moment, we just give him space. I'm not sure if he wants to hear anything at all. But Senne's a great kid. He's got a good head on him. We didn't draw because of him, and we all know that next game he is going to be at the top of his game."

'One mistake from being dropped' - Ashley Young on Senne Lammens

Toni Jimenez is Pochettino's long-time goalkeeping coach.

His arrival triggered the exit of Craig Mawson, who had been with Manchester United since 2019. Connor King is Jimenez's assistant but a relative newcomer himself, having joined from Burnley in 2026.

By its nature, goalkeeping at the highest level can be a mental challenge as well as a technical one. As Onana discovered, flaws can quickly become major issues and once the spotlight is shining, the attention is fierce.

Lammens has given the impression privately of being strong. He has seemed remarkably unaffected by his World Cup torment â his mistake against Spain came after he was introduced as a 71st-minute replacement for injured veteran Thibaut Courtois with the quarter-final delicately poised at 1-1. But only he knows the full picture.

Jimenez will be Pochettino's guide over what to do about the situation, although for now, Lammens' head coach is behind him.

"This type of thing happens," he said. "That is football. Football is about making mistakes.

"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.

"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better."

Following Wednesday's draw in Lisbon, Pochettino highlighted "two things" that need to improve if United are to start winning matches on a regular basis.

The first of those is the club's preferred goalkeeper. Of the 17 Premier League goalkeepers to have played a minimum of 10 matches in all competitions in this campaign, Lammens has the second-worst save success rate, keeping out just 60.2% of the shots he has faced. Only Coventry's Carl Rushworth (54.4%) has fared worse so far this season.

Lammens also ranks bottom of those 17 goalkeepers for clean sheet ratio (6.3%).

And there is substance to the suggestion that Lammens has declined in 2026-27. He made just one error leading to a goal in the entirety of last season in contrast to two already in this campaign. The data also shows that he is currently preventing far fewer goals.

The second "thing", however, has significant bearing on the first.

Clean sheets and conceding fewer goals are clearly a collective responsibility, particularly for the "defensive line" that Pochettino referenced on Wednesday - and United's defence has collectively struggled this season.

They have now let in 36 goals in all competitions, the most of any team in Europe's top five leagues. They have also conceded five penalties and received five red cards - both the second-highest tallies among Europe's elite divisions.

So is Lammens more error-prone this season? Apparently yes. But he's also playing behind a defence that, on current form, may not inspire too much confidence in their goalkeeper.

#903. Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO over extramarital affairs. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators.  Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

It is now one win in seven for Maresca, who cannot keep a clean sheet and has a £327m midfield that have played well individually, but is yet to form a unit. Worryingly, their reliable source of goals, Erling Haaland, had his quietest game of the season. It required Rayan Cherki to rescue a point against Napoli.

Maresca needs to find a solution in the next five days before heading to the Emirates to face the champions in what could be a defining weekend for the season. Defeat would put them nine points off the pace, with Maresca still trying to find his best combination of players to pick.

Club captain Rúben Dias was on the bench here and Josko Gvardiol was left out of the draw against Fulham at the weekend, which also ended as a draw rather than a morale-boosting win to get City out of their slump.

There is enough quality in City’s midfield to trouble Arsenal, but the conundrum for Maresca is how to fit them all into his system. That was a great chance for Napoli. Politano swings in a cross from the right and McTominay has a great headed chance from eight yards but the former Man United man gets his header all wrong. He was actually offside anyway as the linesman’s flag goes up so it would not have counted.

Fernandez’s corner from the left comes all the way to the back post, where he picks out an open Gvardiol. The Croat tries to head it back across goal but it is blocked.

Max Allegri, a manager under pressure, will be reasonably satisfied with the first half an hour away from home for his side. He will though want to see more from his side going forward.

They do create an opening on the right side of the penalty area but Politano’s ball across cannot find a teammate. Politano was put into that good position courtesy of a great first-time pass from De Bruyne.

Two former Manchester United men combine down Napoli’s left as McTominay feeds it forward into the path of Hojlund, whose shot from the left side of the box is straight at Donnarumma.

Napoli have not really threatened the Man City goal and the hosts seem to have a reasonable control on this game but the home fans are very, very quiet and subdued. The only noise really is coming from the away fans. Man City have been a bit slow in possession and have lacked some urgency in their play.

Cherki’s step-over takes him past Lang with ease and is then brought down by the latter just outside the Napoli box on the right. Fernandez fires it low but it is a poor delivery as Gilmour easily clears at the front post.

Haaland goes down inside the Napoli penalty area, wanting a penalty, before Allan has a shot blocked. Olivera had his arms around Haaland as the cross came in from the right but VAR does not intervene. Olivera was taking a risk with that but was the contact enough to take Haaland down to the ground, that is the question?

The travelling Napoli fans are certainly making their voices heard inside the Etihad. They are currently making far more noise than the home supporters.

Enzo Maresca did confirm before the game that Cherki would start wide right and so that has proven. Brazilian forward Allan is out on the left with Fernandez playing in the ten role behind Haaland.

Should O’Reilly have done better with that chance? Nunes clips in a first-time cross from the right which picks out O’Reilly, whose header from eight yards out misses the target.

That was a nervy moment for Man City. Napoli captain Politano clips in a dangerous free-kick from the left to the back post, where McTominay tries to get on the end of it. However, Anderson gets a touch on it before the last touch comes off McTominay. Initially, a corner was given but that is overturned with McTominay touching it last.

Moments later, McTominay has a shot blocked from the left side of the box which goes behind for a corner. De Bruyne, who receives some applause as he goes over to take it, sends the corner too far and the ball goes behind for a goal kick.

The first corner of the night goes the way of the hosts as Anderson’s cross from the right is blocked by Olivera and spins behind for a corner. Interestingly, Napoli have left three players up the pitch.

Man City take it short, with Anderson and Fernandez working it well before the latter has a shot blocked inside the Napoli penalty area.

You would not call Napoli a side in form. Max Allegri’s men have just six wins from 16 games in the league and Champions League so far this season. Manchester City have failed to win any of their last four league games but have won three from four in this competition.

The first chance of the night goes the way of the hosts. Anderson shoots from range and forces Napoli keeper Milinkovic-Savic into a fairly routine save down to his right. Anderson scored a good goal at the weekend in Man City’s draw against Fulham but that effort did not have enough power on it to trouble the Napoli keeper.

Khaldoon Al-Mubarak is here, sat next to Uefa president Aleksander Čeferin.....

After Kevin De Bruyne exchanges plenty of hugs with some former teammates, both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off at the Etihad. A banner for De Bruyne is unveiled. There are a lot of empty seats at the Etihad this evening. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Manchester City: Donnarumma; Nunes, Guéhi, Gvardiol, O’Reilly; Bouaddi, Anderson; Cherki, Fernandez, Allan; Haaland.Substitutes: Rulli, Ndiaye, Kovačić, Doku, Aït-Nouri, Reis, Khusanov, Foden, McAidoo, Samba, Lewis.

Napoli: Milinković-Savić; Beukema, Rrahmani, Olivera; Politano, De Bruyne, Gilmour, McTominay, Spinazzola; Lang; Højlund.Substitutes: Chiummariello, Contini, Lucca, Neres, Giovane, Spinelli, Anguissa.

City will be wearing an orange kit tonight, a special edition in collaboration with fashion brand CP Company. Napoli are also wearing away colours so it will not look much like City v Napoli when they players head out of the tunnel.

How much are Man City missing Kevin De Bruyne? 🤔 Joleon Lescott gives his verdict 👀 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/pogjeOi00P

It is not just Kevin De Bruyne in this Napoli side who is used to the Premier League. In total, there are four former Premier League players in their starting XI; De Bruyne, Rasmus Hojlund, Billy Gilmour and Scott McTominay. On the bench is then former Fulham midfielder André-Frank Zambo Anguissa.

Napoli appear depleted. They have only named seven subs and two of those are goalkeepers. But their midfield has a familiar Premier League look to it with Kevin De Bruyne starting alongside Billy Gilmour and Scott McTominay.

Aston Villa have made the trip out to Istanbul to face Galatasaray and are currently 1-0 down. You can follow the closing stages to that match right here.

Meanwhile in north London, Arsenal host Borussia Dortmund, with that game kicking off at 8pm.

“I am proud of what I have done as a football player, and honestly, this is my club, I love the owners. I have even spoken to [chairman] Khaldoon [Al Mubarak] about how to buy a club. I have nothing but affection for this club, and that will never change, [the way] the people treated me and my family for 10 years.

“Of course, in life there are rules, but everybody plays on the limit. I played in between the white lines, and I competed with other players, and I had many experiences with my teams, with the players. That is the thing that I value most. I have given my all and that is not going to change in my mind. I do not think a lot of people will change in their mind how they view me as a player, or how we played. But everybody has their own opinion, I guess. Other people may be ‘disgraced’ a bit, but I cannot change anything about that.”

Kevin De Bruyne has been lined up for a January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch club working on a deal to land one of the Premier League’s greatest players when the window opens.

De Bruyne, 35, has been at Napoli since the start of last season but it is understood that a move away from the Serie A club is now on the horizon. He is still under contract at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona so PSV will pay a fee to land him as they look to retain their Eredivisie title.

At Manchester City, De Bruyne won six Premier League titles and was part of their Treble-winning team that won the Champions League. During the last 18 months at Napoli he has suffered injury issues, had a row with team-mate on the pitch and was quoted as saying he was glad Antonio Conte left as head coach.

“Not a lot I can say for the moment,” said De Bruyne when asked about his future. “I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

“There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.”

It is matchday five of the Champions League as Manchester City host Napoli at the Etihad. These sides last met back in September 2025, with Manchester City winning 2-0 at home courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku. Manchester City’s cause was helped by an early red card for Napoli’s Giovanni Di Lorenzo. Napoli’s only win over Manchester City came all the way back in November 2011 when they won 2-1 after a double from Edinson Cavani.

Manchester City have won three of their opening four Champions League matches this season, with their only defeat coming at home against back-to-back champions PSG. They drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday, which means they are now without a league win in four games.

“We are always looking to win games, no matter the competition,” Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca said. “For sure, the four games in a row in the Premier League that we did not win has been a shame. Tomorrow [tonight] we have a chance to win the game and continue our path in the Champions League that at the moment has been very good. First of all, it is important to qualify and then probably, if you are not able to finish in the top eight, you have two more games that with the amount of games that we have, it is always important to reduce games. So the target is to try and finish in the top eight.”

Napoli, managed by Massimiliano Allegri, have struggled thus far in this season’s Champions League, winning just one of their opening four games and are all the way down in 27th. They come into tonight’s match off the back of a 1-0 home win over Torino in Serie A on the weekend courtesy of former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay’s winning goal. However, they still sit down in eighth in the Italian top flight, a massive 14 points off the top through just 12 games.

“This match will not be decisive,” Allegri said. “It is a simple mathematical equation, but obviously we will try to do well, even against a great team like Manchester City. It will be a beautiful and fascinating challenge and we want to play to the best of our ability. Ultimately, our goal is to qualify. We must not repeat the mistakes we made in Porto, where we played a great game for 70 minutes and then let ourselves go, conceding chances too easily. We will have to be able to play both with and without possession.”

Team news from the Etihad to follow shortly.

#901. A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains. Credit: 3DMedisphere/SPL

In the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV. Her story could have represented just another sobering statistic in the epidemic that was tearing through the region, but instead, she became a source of inspiration for scientists and of hope for millions. Enrolled in a study to track the course of newly acquired infections, the woman mounted a ferocious immune response to the virus over the next several years as doctors in the study treated her and took regular blood samples to monitor what was going on in her body.

Although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1. The woman is known in the literature as CAP256.

Scientists now think that by mimicking some of the key elements of an infection like hers, they might be able to train other people’s immune systems to make similarly potent antibodies that can block a diverse array of HIV strains. Ultimately, they say, they might achieve one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine that can stop HIV in its tracks.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

“We have a line of sight to an efficacious vaccine,” says Mark Feinberg, president and chief executive of the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) in New York City. “The scientific promise is greater than it’s ever been.”

This year, several teams described vaccination strategies that — in monkeys — can trigger the production of what are known as broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), molecules that can completely shut down an infection from a diverse range of HIV strains before it begins2–4. “No one has achieved that before. It’s a very important milestone,” says Rogier Sanders, a virologist at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

Humans who have received components of similar vaccines can produce precursors to these bnAbs5–7, suggesting that with further refinement, an effective vaccine is possible.

Success is by no means guaranteed, says Feinberg. HIV has proved a formidable foe for vaccine developers in the past. And there is another factor that adds complications. The availability of successful drugs, such as lenacapavir, that prevent HIV infection might make it difficult to test how well a vaccine works. Meanwhile, devastating cuts to the US funding that supported preclinical and clinical research for HIV have left some efforts on a precipice.

“We’re in a better position than we’ve ever been, and just at this time, we’ve seen the funding streams cut off,” says Dennis Burton, an immunologist and virologist at Scripps Research, a research institute in La Jolla, California.

The latest glimmers of success follow decades of failure. Initially, scientists looking to develop an HIV vaccine followed a strategy that had been successful for many other viruses, including hepatitis B: administer a lab-made version of the proteins that viruses use to attach to host cells and the body should start producing antibodies that will block infection. In HIV’s case, it’s the surface protein known as envelope that latches onto a molecular receptor on human T cells so that the virus can infect them. “There was only one protein, and so it seemed straightforward,” says Sallie Permar, a vaccinologist and paediatrician at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York City.

Starting in the 1980s, researchers made vaccines that contained the HIV envelope protein, to elicit antibodies against it, but the vaccines failed to prevent infection in clinical-trial participants. HIV mutates rapidly and most circulating strains were still able to mount an infection. “With HIV, there are millions of strains circulating simultaneously. Taking out one does nothing,” says Richard Wyatt, a viral immunologist at Scripps Research.

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Researchers tried other strategies, such as vaccines that recruited ‘killer’ T cells to wipe out infected cells, and those that delivered a wider diversity of proteins to overcome HIV’s penchant for mutation. In 2009, a clinical trial in Thailand reported modest signs of protection for a vaccine that triggered both T-cell and antibody responses8. But efforts to replicate those results failed, and that strategy was abandoned, too.

One overarching problem, says Feinberg, was that nobody knew what the immunological signature — the measurable biological response after injection — of an effective HIV vaccine looked like, so the only way to assess a candidate was to conduct large-scale efficacy trials and hope for the best. “It was all a shot in the dark,” says Burton.

That attitude began to change after the discovery of bnAbs. In the 1990s, teams led by Burton and microbiologist Hermann Katinger, then at the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences in Vienna, identified the first of them in individuals who were living with HIV9,10. These bnAbs could protect monkeys from infection by HIV strains circulating in Europe and America, but it took large doses, which were unlikely to be reached and sustained with a vaccine. And the protection was less effective against some strains from Africa.

In the 2000s, Burton’s team developed a way to sort through vast numbers of B cells — the immune cells that produce antibodies — for the rare ones that make bnAbs. After screening around 1,800 people living with HIV, they identified a pair of highly potent bnAbs, made by a donor in Africa, that blocked infection from dozens of HIV strains11. “That ignited the field,” says Burton.

Researchers would have to learn how to train the immune system to produce these kinds of bnAb. The strategies to do so emerged from the recognition that bnAbs often develop gradually in HIV-infected individuals such as CAP256. It happens through a sustained “cat and mouse game” between the fast-changing virus and an immune system struggling to keep up, says Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases and the University of Witwatersrand, both in Johannesburg, who analysed CAP256’s blood.

To mimic that struggle in an uninfected person, researchers first deliver a ‘priming’ immunogen — a portion or complete copy of HIV’s envelope. This shot awakens B cells, triggering them to divide and become active. Subsequent doses deliver distinct versions of the HIV envelope to first ‘shape’ and then ‘polish’ the antibodies produced. The goal is to guide the awakened B cells through a process called affinity maturation, in which the antibodies develop extensive mutations that improve their binding and breadth. The key is that the most capable B cells are recruited early and the antibodies that they produce are honed over time (see ‘Targeted vaccines’).

Source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

Sanders says that this strategy, sometimes known as germline targeting, is a bit like looking for an elite footballer among pools of youth players. Rather than trying to train everyone up to an expert level, they want to identify talent early and nurture it to superstardom. “We’re scouting the talented B cells,” Sanders says.

Researchers have taken different approaches to scouting these cells. After Moore and colleagues discovered CAP256’s antibodies, they sequenced the viruses circulating in her blood to identify what might have triggered and shaped the antibodies’ production.

A modified version of the envelope protein from one such virus has shown promise as a priming agent for the immune system in monkeys and is now being trialled in humans, says virologist George Shaw who co-led the preclinical work for this2 with virologist Beatrice Hahn, both at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

Another team, led by William Schief at Scripps Research, used computational structural modelling and cell studies to design immunogens that activate a specific subset of B cells that make antibodies capable of blocking the binding site through which HIV latches onto T cells5.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants

In small trials of vaccination with either protein or mRNA-based versions of this immunogen12, which is called eOD-GT8, nearly all participants developed ‘bnAb precursors’. These are antibodies with the desired genetic and structural characteristics of a bnAb that blocks the T-cell binding site on the envelope protein, but not the bevy of mutations that makes bnAbs elite. In participants who also got a booster shot of a different immunogen, the antibodies picked up mutations that improved their binding and neutralization abilities. “It worked beautifully,” says Schief, who is also vice-president for protein design at Moderna Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

#900. Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir

Written and smuggled out of prison, the 2023 Nobel Prize laureate's memoir reveals the cost of defying Iran's regime and fighting for freedom.

As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.

"A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.

The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.

Mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," says Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over."

But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety.

In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism.

The human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection.

Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s.

In "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities.

She began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community.

In 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani. The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006.

Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi.

She played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights.

Her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life.

In her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months.

She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care.

Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project "White Torture."

"When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely."

"This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes.

Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these issues to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists.

International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all."

As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world.

Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue new legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison.

She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats.

"We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," says Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it."

In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health.

Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances.

In prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons."

But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison.

In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban.

Mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is currently subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?"

Despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the issue of human rights in Iran in the public eye, says Claren: "It is incredibly important that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance."

#899. The local boy aiming to be at the heart of Cardiff's derby aims

Colwill has one goal and three assists from 10 Championship appearances following Cardiff City's return to the Championship

Rubin Colwill is used to being in the centre of things.

He has been the focus of an ongoing argument over his role - or lack of it - in Craig Bellamy's Wales side.

It has meant the midfielder has been the subject of countless questions around international weeks, the latest prompting the Wales boss to ask a journalist if he had a Colwill poster in the middle of his bedroom wall.

The debate has stemmed from the 24-year-old being at the heart of Brian Barry-Murphy's stylish transformation of Cardiff City.

So it is understandable that, as he prepares to lead his boyhood club into the eye of the storm that is the south Wales derby, he is again in the centre of things.

And fitting for someone who grew up in the middle of the rivalry between the two cities.

"I took a lot of stick," Colwill said. Well, we presume that is what he might have said, stopping himself from swearing to describe life as a Cardiff fan from the town of Neath, nine miles from Swansea.

"I probably felt it more than most being surrounded by Swansea fans and a lot of mates being Swansea fans.

"It was tough because they were in the Premier League for a long spell, so I was always trying to give a bit back when we won a game or did well."

Bellamy an influence as Williams leads Swansea

Bellamy jokes reporter has Colwill poster in bedroom

Latest Cardiff City news, analysis and fan views

Colwill was always Cardiff, as was brother Joel, his team-mate for club and country.

Their mother - from Port Talbot, a little further east with a denser amount of support that turn towards the capital - was a Cardiff fan and so were her boys, signing for the club while still in primary school.

He has never gone to a derby in Swansea as a fan - he was never allowed - but was part of the Cardiff side that last won at their rivals in 2021 and has told team-mates all about the journey down the M4, where fans flock to bridges and encouragement turns to abuse as the miles clock up.

He will mention that, and the feeling of the times where, by his own admission, Cardiff were not good enough in a string of defeats that sting more than most.

But he will also share the "no better" feeling of being in the middle of the celebrations of a derby win, as he was in January 2025.

Colwill: 'Tough' growing up as a Cardiff fan

That Cardiff 3-0 victory was a rare high point in a season that eventually saw the club relegated from the Championship and in desperate need of a rebuild.

They have done just that, transitioning into an eye-catching, exciting team, who - depsite failing to win away this season and going into the game on the back of a 4-0 defeat by Preston North End - are ready to show Swansea the Bluebirds are a different beast these days.

Colwill and his influence has been very much a central cog in that change.

He has been game time and responsibility by Barry-Murphy - including the armband that might not be obvious for such a seemingly laidback character.

The academy product says he has learned much from the journey, including a frustrating spell of injuries that have limited his impact to seven starts since the return to the Championship.

It has seemingly been noticed by Bellamy, who spoke before Wales' recent Nations League defeat to Portugal about how he has improved as a player.

"There has been a big change in his game," Bellamy said, a former academy coach of the talented midfielder.

"He is a player I really like watching - before I did and I didn't. Now I see a lot of good things."

Colwill responded with a man-of-the-match performance against Portugal in what was his first competitive Wales start in five years.

"It was almost like I got to experience my first game twice," smiled Colwill.

Bellamy - who has questioned Colwill's work off the ball - has said he felt able to be more "ruthless" with the youngster because of their long association.

"Everyone knows," said Bellamy of what he thought Colwill needed to do to improve. "And none more than him."

Williams to lead Swansea in south Wales derby

Frozen out Robinson told he has Cardiff future

Despite being in the middle of it all, Colwill has not changed in playing personality, and certainly showed no pressure when he reclaimed his Wales spot.

Clearly there is a resilience that goes beyond sticking with a Cardiff scarf in an area full of Swansea colours.

"I've tried to learn from those experiences and develop myself mentally and improve my resilience so I can almost take anything that comes my way," he says.

"I think that's a massive part of football: you've got to stay grounded, stay focused, regardless if you're doing really well or really badly because it's a massive part of the game to stay consistent in the end."

So what of the challenge to improve and being in the middle of the two different approaches to getting the most out of him?

"I think they're very similar," is Colwill's response. "They both want to control the game, the structure, the body shape, how they want us to play, the press and reaction to giving the ball away.

"In the fundamentals of the game, they're similar. Obviously they're both different people so the approaches to that are very different, and it's in the little details.

"With Craig, he's always had that approach of if he thinks you can offer something or improve on, it's on us to take it on board and be open to that constructive criticism.

"It's not always easy. I think he does have a high demand of you, but if you do make a change as he asks of you then he will play you."

Cardiff players will have 'edge' against Swansea

After the stick, the carrot at Cardiff is the chance to follow in Bellamy's footsteps by scoring a winner in the derby at Swansea, as the Wales boss did in 2011 - Cardiff's last win there in front of travelling supporters.

Colwill smiles at the thought, just as he winces at the memories of the defeats - as a player and a fan - which is why he will not be telling team-mates to treat this game like just another.

"That attitude is almost like trying to protect yourself from the pressure," he argues. "But it's not. We have a lot of boys from the area who have come from the academy who really get the game and understand the whole picture of it and how important it is for everyone in the city.

"And we've got no fear of failure - if we lose we just leave it all out there, but we have full belief we can win."

If they do, it will come as no surprise if Colwill is at the heart of it.

#898. Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even launches?

The TFFF rainforest fund aims to make forest conservation more profitable than deforestation. But a lack of money may prevent it from getting off the ground.

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

More recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the plan is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner said, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform launched by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner said the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner said.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner said.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

"Promises like that always come at the last minute," he said. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion."

This article was originally written in German.
